title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-321-528
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-321-528; 5-292-982
Stipulations
1. The parties have stipulated that claimant’s average weekly wage is $2,076
per week and the TTD rate is $1,338.96 per week.
2. If the matter is found compensable, the parties have agreed that liability for
temporary benefits would commence on December 10, 2024. The amount due claimant
is unknown at this time, pending information regarding offsets or other income. During
hearing, claimant did indicate that he has received unemployment benefits during this
period.
3. The parties have stipulated that proposed lumbar decompression is
reasonable and necessary for claimant, but not that it is related to the work event of
October 31, 2024.
Issues
The following issues were raised for consideration at hearing:
Whether claimant has carried his burden to prove that a disc extrusion at L5-S1
⮚
was caused by an incident at work on October 31, 2024.
Whether surgery in the form of lumbar decompression at L5-S1 is related to an
⮚
incident at work on October 31, 2024.
Dismissal of W.C. No. 5-292-982, date of injury November 19, 2024, with
⮚
prejudice.
Whether respondents are responsible for one and a half hours billed by ATP Dr.
⮚
Waksehima for a records review and special report requested by claimant.
1

Findings of Fact
1. Claimant was employed by Choice Electric, LLC as a journeyman
electrician and foreman. Choice Electric is an electrical contractor that performs
electrical installations on industrial and commercial building projects.
2. Claimant was hired by Choice Electric on March 11, 2013, and had been
continuously employed with the company for approximately thirteen years at the
time of the lifting and bending incident on October 31, 2024. Claimant was a full-
time, regular employee. He claims a work injury occurred to his back on October
31, 2024. He claims he was working at Denver International Airport carrying
Electrical Metallic Tubing (EMT) from outside the airport building and carrying
them inside to install in a restaurant located in one of the concourses. This
involved carrying bundles which contained ten individual ten-foot-long pieces of
pipe. Each bundle weighed 70 to 80 pounds. There were seven bundles. He
carried each bundle on his shoulder while navigating around multiple ropes that
were in place to coordinate passenger traffic to aircraft boarding areas. He would
have to duck under each rope barrier carrying the bundles. On approximately the
third trip carrying a bundle, Claimant bent back while ducking under a rope, he
felt a "tweak" in his lower back on the left side. Claimant described the sensation
as a sharp pain that "didn't feel right," like he had "bent the wrong way”. He
testified that he felt a pinch in his left leg, as if a muscle was pinched or pulled.
3. On December 6, 2024, claimant testified that he called his employer and told them
that he needed to be seen by a doctor. He admits that he did not indicate to them
that there was a work-related injury associated with this need to see a doctor. He
called for an appointment with his Primary Care Physician (PCP) and was seen
that afternoon. Claimant had last been seen by this provider on November 5, 2024
and did not raise the issue of a work-related injury at that time. The December 6,
2

2024 visit was the initial visit regarding what he now asserts is a work injury. The
history given to his PCP on the December 6, 2024 visit was “pt woke up 3 weeks
ago and c/o left gluteal pain, took 800mg of ibuprofen which helped, he’s been
having intermittent left gluteal pain since then and it shoots down his leg into his
left foot. No recent trauma. Occupation: electrician journeyman”. He was provided
a prescription for a Medrol dose pack.
4. The medical records for a date of visit of December 6, 2024 indicate that his
symptoms three weeks prior was the “first time this happened to patient”. A
return to work note was provided.
5. Claimant returned to his PCP after the completion of his steroid prescription on
December 12, 2024. He reported that the steroid pack helped for one day where
he felt no pain, but returned the day after. He said Gabapentin didn’t help at all. He
appeared at this appointment in a wheel chair. Despite being in a wheel chair
because of what he now identifies as a work incident, he still provided no history
of a work event leading to his condition and complaints. No trauma was noted. A
STAT referral was made to an orthopedic spine surgeon. Arrangements were
made and he was scheduled for labs at 7:30 a.m. the next morning, December 13,
2024. Follow up appointments were made. There was still no report to the
employer of a work injury, despite the significant concern and the STAT
appointments.
6. Claimant was seen at Spine One Spine & Sports Medicine Center the next day,
Friday, December 13, 2024. There continued to be no reference to a work injury.
Claimant was complaining of pain 10/10 and that he presented with “4 weeks of
3

severe low back pain radiating to the left lower extremity.” He said he was in
pain all day with all movement. These records say his symptoms began 4 weeks
ago “without any specific event but he does attribute it to his work as an
electrician”. The evaluator indicated that it was necessary to obtain a lumbar
MRI, and that “At this time, the patient appears to be a candidate for potential
spine intervention once imaging has been obtained for procedural planning.”
7. Claimant did not contact the employer to report an injury until this reference to
possible surgery was made. “He then decided to put his injury under Workers’
Comp”. He testified that he contacted his employer after this appointment on
Friday December 13, 2024. He was sent a form to report the injury by early
Monday, December 16, 2024.
8. Dr. Allison Fall was admitted as an expert. She is Level II accredited, has been
trained in the Division recommendations for causation analysis, and along with
her M.D., has a BA in biomedical engineering. She testified that claimant’s
condition can be caused without an acute incident, and frequently does.
Movement during sleep is frequently used as an example of an innocuous cause
for a disc extrusion. She testified that the history given on December 6, 2024,
that he woke up with symptoms, is a medically reasonable and probable
explanation for claimant’s condition. It is noted that the providers on December
6, 12 and 13 did not indicate they were confused or found the history given to be
inadequate to explain claimant’s condition. They also found the “waking up with
the problem” mechanism to be a probable cause of claimant’s condition. Dr. Fall
testified the timing of the mechanism of injury is part of the consideration when
evaluating causation. If the injury had occurred on October 31, 2024, claimant
would not have delayed seeking treatment for 36 days. He would not have
4

confused an onset “three weeks” before December 6, 2024 with one 36 days
before. She explained that an extrusion is different from a herniation. The
extrusion is some of the interior material from the disc that has fully pulled away
from the disc. In claimant’s case, an extrusion of disc material is impinging upon
the nerve. The normal course of the nerve is changed by the disc pushing upon
it. This is a painful condition, and does not take a long time to progress. She
testified that in claimant’s case, the displacement of the nerve would cause
symptoms in a short period of time, as opposed to a herniation only. This is not a
matter of late reporting, it is a matter of causation and medical probability, in light
of the early medical records. None of the three early reports with the PCP
support a work injury. There was also a visit on November 5, 2024 – between
October 31, 2024 and December 6, 2024 - that had no indication of injury. The
December 6, 2024 visit was clear that these complaints were new and had not
happened before. Dr. Fall testified that the earlier records are more medically
likely to be the most accurate and have greater weight when assessing
causation. She testified that she does not see any clinical evidence in the
medical records through the December 13, 2024 Spine One visit that support a
work injury.
9. Claimant brought his Claimant’s IME report and Dr. Fall’s report to his ATP Dr.
Wakeshima and he and his attorney requested that the doctor provide a special
report with his determination of which he found “persuasive.” Records reflect
discussion and questions posed by both claimant and his attorney and that Dr.
Wakeshima provide a report that could be used to advocate for claimant’s
5

position at hearing. Stepping into the fact finder role, Dr. Wakeshima provided
his conclusions in favor of claimant’s position. He spent an hour and a half on
this work. There was no request by respondents and no agreement with
respondents that his time be spent with this records review and special report.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S. is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law
judge. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637
(Colo. App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a
contrary inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make
credibility determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at
641. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions;
the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
6

testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has
been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Ins. Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert
testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is
subject to conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting
part or none of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n,
441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
D. The December 6, 2024 visit was the initial visit regarding how the onset of
symptoms happened. Although he mentioned his occupation, he did not attribute
his symptoms to any work-related activity. Claimant returned to his PCP after the
completion of his steroid prescription on December 12, 2024. He reported that the
steroid pack helped for one day where he felt no pain, but returned the day after.
He said Gabapentin didn’t help at all. He appeared at this appointment in a wheel
chair. Despite being in a wheelchair because of what he now identifies as a work
incident, he still provided no history of a work event leading to his condition and
complaints. No trauma was noted. A STAT referral was made to an orthopedic
spine surgeon. Arrangements were made and he was scheduled for labs at 7:30
a.m. the next morning, December 13, 2024. Follow up appointments were made.
There was still no report to the employer of a work injury, despite the significant
7

concern and the STAT appointments.
E. Claimant was seen at Spine One Spine & Sports Medicine Center the next day,
Friday, December 13, 2024. There continued to be no reference to a work injury.
Claimant was complaining of pain 10/10 and that he had been experience “4
weeks of severe low back pain radiating to the left lower extremity.” He said he
was in pain all day with all movement. These records say his symptoms began 4
weeks ago “without any specific event but he does attribute it to his work as an
electrician”. The evaluator indicated that it was necessary to obtain an lumbar
MRI, and that “At this time, the patient appears to be a candidate for potential
spine intervention once imaging has been obtained for procedural planning.”
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. By agreement of Claimant, W.C. 5-292-982 is withdrawn and dismissed with
prejudice
2. The claim for compensation in W.C. 321-528 is denied and dismissed.
3. Respondents are not liable for the report generated by Dr. Wakeshima at the
request of Claimant.
NOTE: If you are dissatisfied with the ALJ's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on the certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the ALJ's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it
within twenty (20) days after mailing or service of the order of the ALJ; and (2) That you
mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. You may
file your Petition to Review electronically by emailing the Petition to Review to the
following email address: oac-ptr@state.co.us. If the Petition to Review is emailed to the
aforementioned email address, the Petition to Review is deemed filed in Denver
8

pursuant to OACRP 27 and Section 8-43-301, C.R.S. If the Petition to Review is filed
by email to the proper email address, it does not need to be mailed to the Denver Office
of Administrative Courts. For further information regarding procedures to follow when
filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may access a petition to review
form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.

title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-317-741-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-317-741-001
Stipulation of Facts
1. The Claimant in this matter, , was born on March 5, 1989.
Claimant resides in Colorado Springs Colorado.
2. The Claimant was employed by and performing metal building construction type
work for the Respondent Employer on and before September 11, 2025. On
September 11, 2025, while on a job site in Pueblo Colorado on behalf of the
Respondent at approximately 9:00 a.m. the Claimant fell to the ground from the
roof. The fall was approximately 16 feet. Clamant struck the ground with both hands
as well as his face.
3. Due to the fall the Claimant sustained injuries and was transported by co-workers
present at the site to St. Mary Corwin Hospital in Pueblo Colorado. At the Hospital
the claimant was casted, fingers fixated and he was provided with pain medication.
Claimant reported injury to bilateral wrists, hands and fingers as well as his face and
jaw.
4. , a principal of the Respondent/Employer, became aware of the fall and
went to the hospital and saw the Claimant there. was aware that the
Claimant sustained injuries but took no other action and did not provide the Claimant
a name of a provider or a workers’ compensation insurance carrier.
5. On September 11, 2025, the Claimant was employed to work in the metal building
construction business of the Respondent/Employer, J & B Construction. The
Claimant was paid for the services he provided by check drawn on an account of J &
B Construction. Copies of these checks are entered into evidence as Exhibit 2 and are
signed by and reference job sites. The checks were made payable to the
Claimant in his name. No withholdings, including federal or state taxes or FICA were

Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S. is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law
judge. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637
(Colo. App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a
contrary inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make
credibility determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at
641. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions;
the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has
been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Ins. Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert
testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is
subject to conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting
6

part or none of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n,
441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
D. The ALJ concludes that the Claimant performed services for the Employer for
pay and at the time of the injury the employee was performing services arising
out of and in the course of the employee’s employment with the Employer. The
ALJ concludes that the injuries suffered Claimant suffered on September 11,
2025, are compensable.
E. An employer is liable for medical treatment reasonably necessary to cure and
relieve the effects of an industrial injury. Section 8-42-101. Under § 8-43-404(5),
the employer has the right to choose the treating physician in the first instance.
But the employer must tender medical treatment “forthwith” upon receiving notice
of the injury, or the right of selection passes to the claimant. Rogers v. Industrial
Claim Appeals Office, 746 P.2d 565 (Colo. App. 1987).
F. Employer never referred Claimant to a specific physician or clinic, so the right of
selection passed to Claimant. Employer is responsible for the evaluations and
treatment Claimant has received to date at St. Mary Corwin Hospital and St.
Mary Corwin Orthopedic for to relieve and cure the claimant from the effects of
the injury of September 11, 2025.
G. A claimant may obtain permission to treat with a physician of their choosing
“upon the proper showing to the division.” Section 8-43-404(5)(a)(VI)(A);
Gianetto Oil Co. v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 931 P.2d 570 (Colo. App.
1996). Section 8-43-404(5)(a)(VI)(A) does not define a “proper showing,” and
the ALJ has broad discretion to decide if the circumstances justify a change or
addition of an ATP. Jones v. T.T.C. Illinois, Inc., W.C. No. 4-503-150 (May 5,
7

2006). The ALJ may consider a wide range of factors including whether the
claimant has received adequate treatment, whether the claimant trusts the
ATP, the level of communication between the claimant and the ATP, the ATP’s
expertise and skill at managing a condition, and the ATP’s willingness to provide
additional treatment. E.g., Carson v. Wal-Mart, W.C. No. 3-964-07 (April 12,
1993); Merrill v. Mulberry Inn, Inc., W.C. No. 3-949-781 (November 1995);
Greenwalt-Beltmain v. Department of Regulatory Agencies, W.C. No. 3-896-
932 (December 5, 1995); Zimmerman v. United Parcel Service, W.C. No. 4-
018-264 (August 23, 1995).
The parties have stipulated that effective on the date of this Order Dr. Miguel
Castrejon will become authorized to provide treatment to the Claimant. This is
hereby accepted.
H. C.R.S. §8-42-102(2) provides compensation shall be based on the
employee’s average weekly earnings “at the time of the injury.” The statute
sets forth several computational methods for workers paid on an hourly, salary,
per diem basis, etc. But § 8-42-102(3) gives the ALJ wide discretion to “fairly”
calculate the employee’s AWW in any manner that seems most appropriate
under the circumstances. The entire objective of AWW calculation is to arrive
at a “fair approximation” of the claimant’s actual wage loss and diminished
earning capacity because of the industrial injury. Campbell v. IBM Corp., 867
P.2d 77 (Colo. App. 1993). As found, Claimant’s AWW is $1500, with a
corresponding TTD rate of $1,000.00.
I. A claimant is entitled to temporary disability benefits if the injury causes a
disability, the disability causes the claimant to leave work, and the claimant
misses more than three regular working days. PDM Molding, Inc. v. Stanberg,
898 P.2d 542 (Colo. 1995). The claimant must establish a causal connection
between a work-related injury and the wage loss to obtain disability benefits. Id.
The term disability connotes two elements: (1) medical incapacity evidenced by
loss or restriction of bodily function, and (2) impairment of wage-earning capacity
8

as demonstrated by claimant's inability to resume his prior work. Culver v. Ace
Electric, 971 P.2d 641 (Colo. 1999). Impairment of earning capacity may be
evidenced by a complete inability to work, or by restrictions that impair the
claimant's ability effectively and properly to perform her regular employment.
Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy & Co., 964 P.2d 595 (Colo. App. 1998). Once
commenced, disability benefits continue until the occurrence of one of the factors
enumerated in § 8-42-105(3), C.R.S.
J. The unrefuted evidence shows Claimant was disabled by his industrial injury and

K. Claimant seeks a penalty under § 8-43-203 for “failure to file [a] General
Admission of Liability.” The employer must admit or deny liability within 20 days
after it learns of an injury that results in “lost time from work for the injured
employee in excess of three shifts or calendar days.” Section 8-43-101; 8-43-
203(1)(a). Under § 8-43-203(2)(a), an employer “may become liable” to the
claimant “for up to one day’s compensation for each day’s failure” to file an
admission or notice of contest with the Division. The maximum penalty for failure
to admit or deny liability cannot exceed “the aggregate amount of three hundred
sixty-five days’ compensation.” Fifty percent of any penalty shall be paid to the
claimant and fifty percent to the Subsequent Injury Fund. Section 8-43-203(2)(a),
C.R.S.
L. The phrase “may become liable” means imposition of a penalty under § 8-43-
203(2)(a) is discretionary. E.g., Gebrekidan v. MKBS, LLC, W.C. No. 4-678-723
(May 10, 2007). The purposes of the requirement to admit or deny liability are to
notify the claimant he is involved in a proceeding with legal ramifications, and to
notify the Division of the employer’s position so the Division can exercise its
9

administrative oversight over the claim process. Smith v. Myron Stratton Home,
676 P.2d 1196 (Colo. 1984). Two important purposes of penalties are to punish
the violator and deter future misconduct. May v. Colorado Civil Rights
Commission, 43 P.3d 750 (Colo. App. 2002). The ALJ should consider factors
such as the reprehensibility of the conduct and the extent of harm to the non-
violating party. Associated Business Products v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office,
126 P.3d 323 (Colo. App. 2005). The penalty should not be constitutionally
excessive or grossly disproportionate to the violation found. Dami Hospitality,
LLC v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 442 P.3d 94 (Colo. 2019). The claimant
must prove circumstances justifying the imposition of a penalty. Pioneer Hospital
v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 114 P.3d 97 (Colo. App. 2005).
M. Employer knew Claimant suffered a lost time injury on September 11, 2025, so
the deadline to admit or deny liability was October 1, 2025. Employer did not file
an admission or denial of liability until an appearance at a Division of Workers’
Compensation Pre-Hearing Conference held on January 21, 2026. The Employer
has never provided any support for the Claimant. Besides providing a remedy to
the claimant, § 8-43-203 serves a public purpose of apprising the Division of the
claim and encouraging employers to follow the procedures set forth in the
Workers’ Compensation Act. As such, some penalty is warranted to promote and
reinforce the integrity of the system, irrespective of any harm to Claimant.
N. Based on the facts of this case, Employer should be penalized $30 per day from
October 1, 2025 through January 21, 2026. Fifty percent (50%) of this penalty
shall be paid to Claimant and fifty percent (50%) to the Subsequent Injury Fund.

paid or ordered . . . an employer who is not in compliance with the insurance

P. The penalty for failure to insure only applies to indemnity benefits; it does not
apply to medical benefits. Industrial Commission v. Hammond, 77 Colo. 414, 236
P. 1006 (1925); Jacobson v. Doan, 319 P.2d 975 (Colo. 1957); Wolford v.
Support, Inc., W.C. No. 4-155- 231 (February 13, 1998). Although the ALJ is not

during the accrual period. Subsequent Injury Fund v. Trevethan, 809 P.2d 1098
(Colo. App. 1991). Similarly, the ALJ concludes that the penalties awarded herein
are not “compensation or benefits.”

intention to state that the cart incident happened on November 13, 2023.
12. On November 16, 2023, Claimant was seen by Dr. Robert James
McLaughlin. At that time, Dr. McLaughlin became Claimant’s authorized treating
provider (ATP) for this claim. On November 16, 2023, Dr. McLaughlin recorded the
following “[Claimant] reports [two] months ago she was at work, and she was pushing a
cart. The wheels got stuck as there was [sic] sideways to a crack. There was also a little
elevation ago [sic]. She kept pushing it back and forth. . .” Claimant also reported to Dr.
McLaughlin that since that incident she had worsening right elbow pain. Dr. McLaughlin
diagnosed a right elbow strain. Dr. McLaughlin also noted that Claimant experienced an
acute event. In addition, Dr. McLaughlin opined that his objective findings were
consistent with a work-related mechanism of injury. Dr. McLaughlin referred Claimant to
occupational therapy and assigned work restrictions. Thereafter, Claimant continued to
treat with Dr. McLaughlin throughout this claim.
3

13. On December 5, 2023, Claimant attended occupational therapy with Lynn
Hatfield Harrison, OTR. At that time Therapist Hatfield Harrison recorded that Claimant
had several months of right elbow pain that was “exacerbated when she was trying to
push a cart on wheels that got stuck and she had to push/pull it back/forth several times
to loosen it.”
14. On January 8, 2024, Respondents filed a General Admission of Liability,
admitting liability for Claimant’s work injury.
15. On January 16, 2024, Claimant returned to Therapist Hatfield Harrison. At
that time, it was noted that Claimant had not progressed despite having undergone
therapy and acupuncture. Therapist Hatfield Harrison opined that if Claimant did not
progress over the next three to four weeks, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or a
referral to orthopedics might be warranted.
16. Claimant was seen by Dr. McLaughlin on February 13, 2024. At that time,
Dr. McLaughlin noted that Claimant’s symptoms continued to fluctuate for unknown
reasons, and progress was extremely slow. Dr. McLauglin ordered an MRI of Claimant’s
right upper extremity, and additional occupational therapy.
17. On March 9, 2024, Claimant underwent an MRI of her right elbow. The
MRI showed, inter alia, moderate lateral epicondylitis change of the common extensor
origin; thickening and edematous change to the common extensor tendon complex,
some proximal edema of the extensor carpi radialis brevis musculature; osteochondral
degeneration at the posterior capitellum bare area junction; and small joint effusion. The
radiologist, Dr. Frank Crnkovich also noted edematous change of the brachialis muscle
belly; proximal myotendinous margin; and tendinosis change without disruption.
18. After reviewing the MRI results, on March 11, 2024, Dr. McLaughlin
referred Claimant for an orthopedic consultation.
19. On April 1, 2024, Claimant was seen at Orthopedic Centers of Colorado
by Dr. Lauren MacTaggart. In the medical record of that date, Claimant’s symptoms
4

were recorded as mild to moderate and fluctuating, with a deep ache that is throbbing
and sharp. Dr. MacTaggart noted that Claimant was injured when she was attempting to
move a cart at work. Dr. MacTaggart diagnosed Claimant with right elbow lateral
epicondylitis. At that time, Dr. MacTaggart recommended continued physical therapy
that would include dry needling.
20. On July 29, 2024, Claimant returned to Dr. MacTaggart and reported that
initially dry needling helped, but then as the treatment continued her symptoms
worsened. Claimant also reported approximately 70 percent improvement in her
symptoms since the injury. Dr. MacTaggart recommended Claimant undergo a
diagnostic ultrasound with consideration of possible PRP2 injections.
21. On September 11, 2024, Claimant was seen at Orthopedic Centers of
Colorado by Dr. Efren Caballes. In the medical record of that date, Dr. Caballes
referenced an “injury to [Claimant’s] elbow while pushing a heavy cart”. Dr. Caballes
also recorded ten months of “gradual onset in the setting of repetitive use at work”. On
examination, Dr. Caballes noted reproducible lateral elbow pain. Dr. Caballes
recommended PRP injection to the common extensor tendon and radiocapitellar joint of
the right elbow.
22. On September 26, 2024, Dr. Caballes administered the recommended
PRP injection.
23. On November 6, 2024, Claimant returned to Dr. Caballes and reported
that her symptoms were “relatively unchanged”. Claimant also reported that due to her
continued symptoms she was unable to do her physical therapy exercises with
resistance. Dr. Caballes performed an ultrasound exam and noted resolution of
synovitis in the radiocapitellar joint, and unchanged condition of the common extensor
tendon. Dr. Caballes opined that Claimant would have a “slow healing course” and
recommended a therapy focused on “soft tissue mobilization and progressive loading”.
2 Platelet rich plasma.
5

24. Claimant was seen by Dr. McLaughlin on November 26, 2024. At that
time, Claimant reported that she was better since her prior visit. Dr. McLaughlin opined
that “there is not much more else [sic] I think that can really be done.” He recommended
Claimant complete her final session of occupational therapy and follow-up with Dr.
Caballes.
25. On December 20, 2024, Claimant was seen by Dr. Caballes and reported
gradual improvement of her symptoms. Dr. Caballes performed an ultrasound and noted
resolution of synovitis in the radiocapitellar joint, with improvement of the common
extensor tendon. In addition, Dr. Caballes stated that Claimant could return to all
activities, as tolerated. He recommended that Claimant follow-up with her occupational
medicine providers.
26. On April 14, 2025, Claimant returned to Dr. McLaughlin and reported that
her symptoms were somewhat better. However, she also reported difficulty with
sleeping, cleaning, and cooking. As a result, she often used her left hand to complete
tasks. Dr. McLaughlin opined that as of that date (April 14, 2025), Claimant had reached
maximum medical improvement (MMI) for her right elbow injury. Dr. McLaughlin
assessed a permanent impairment rating of 11 percent for Claimant’s right upper
extremity (which converts to seven percent whole person). With regard to post-MMI
treatment, Dr. McLaughlin recommended follow-ups for medications, continued use of a
topical patch, possible additional injections, and follow-up with orthopedic and pain
management providers. Additionally, Dr. McLaughlin assigned permanent work
restrictions that included no repetitive motion with the right arm, wrist, and elbow;
maximum lifting, pushing, and pulling of five pounds; and a two-pound restriction for
routine lifting, pushing, and pulling.
27. At the request of Respondents, Claimant was scheduled to attend an
independent medical examination (IME) with Dr. Carlos Cebrian on April 24, 2025.
However, an interpreter was not available at that time, resulting in rescheduling of the
IME. As a result, Dr. Cebrian performed a review of Claimant’s medical records. In a
report dated May 23, 2025, Dr. Cebrian opined that Claimant did not suffer a work-
6

related injury. Dr. Cebrian further opined that the causation analysis related to
Claimant’s condition should have been done as a cumulative trauma analysis and not
that of an acute injury. Dr. Cebrian explained that if a cumulative trauma analysis is
done, then Claimant does not have a compensable condition. In support of this opinion,
Dr. Cebrian noted that Claimant’s job duties do not have primary or secondary factors
that would support an occupational exposure or repetitive motion type injury. Dr.
Cebrian also expressed concerns with the timing of the onset and reporting of
Claimant’s symptoms.
28. On August 4, 2025, Claimant was seen by Dr. McLaughlin for a post-MMI
maintenance medical visit. At that time, Dr. McLaughlin noted that Claimant was having
difficulty with her activities of daily living including sleeping, driving, and eating. Dr.
McLaughlin recommended that she return to Dr. Caballes. Dr. McLaughlin specifically
referenced the possibility of additional injections.
29. Respondents requested a Division sponsored independent medical
examination (DIME). On September 10, 2025, Claimant attended a DIME with Dr.
Matthew Delarosa. In connection with the DIME, Dr. Delarosa reviewed Claimant’s
medical records, obtained a history from Claimant, and performed a physical
examination. In his DIME report, Dr. Delarosa opined that Claimant had been correctly
diagnosed with lateral epicondylitis. Dr. Delarosa also noted that “causality has been
well established” It was also Dr. Delarosa’s opinion that Claimant not yet at MMI as
further treatment options were available. Specifically, Dr. Delarosa opined that
Claimant was a candidate for surgical intervention that would include lateral
epicondylitis debridement and reattachment. Although Dr. Delarosa determined
Claimant was not at MMI, he assessed a provisional permanent impairment rating of 22
percent for Claimant’s right upper extremity (which converts to 13 percent, whole
person). The basis for this rating was two percent for range of motion, and 20 percent
for loss of grip strength.
30. On February 26, 2026, Claimant attended an IME with Dr. Cebrian. As he
had previously reviewed Claimant’s medical records, the IME included obtaining a
7

history from Claimant and performed a physical examination. In his March 18, 2026 IME
report, Dr. Cebrian reiterated his opinions from the May 23, 2025 report.
31. On March 14, 2026, Claimant underwent a right elbow MRI. That MRI
showed mild to moderate common extensor tendinosis with minimal interstitial tearing;
and mild insertional triceps tendinosis. In the MRI report, Dr. Gregory Tomc specifically
noted that it was an “[o]therwise unremarkable right elbow MRI.”
32. On March 24, 2026, Claimant was seen at Orthopedic Centers of
Colorado by Dr. Sean Griggs. In that record, Dr. Griggs describes Claimant’s
mechanism of injury as “[Claimant] was pushing a heavy cart. She had sharp pain down
her arm.” Dr. Griggs diagnosed Claimant with right lateral epicondylitis “with failure of
conservative management including therapy, PRP injection and over [two] years of
conservative management.” Dr. Griggs opined that Claimant was a candidate for
additional PRP injections, steroid injection, or surgery. After discussion, Claimant
elected to pursue surgical intervention. Specifically, Dr. Griggs recommended a right
lateral epicondylitis debridement with repair.
33. After his review of Dr. Griggs’s March 24, 2026 report, Dr. McLaughlin
issued his own report on March 30, 2026. Dr. McLaughlin noted the recent MRI results
and Dr. Griggs’s recommendation for surgery. In that report, Dr. McLaughlin reiterated
his opinion that Claimant suffered an acute and work-related injury to her right elbow.
Dr. McLaughlin also identified Dr. Delarosa as an “orthopedic upper extremity specialist”
who had also opined that Claimant was a surgical candidate. Dr. McLaughlin also stated
that he agreed with Drs. Griggs and Delarosa that Claimant was not at MMI. He further
stated that, in his opinion, the surgery recommended by Dr. Griggs is reasonable and
necessary medical treatment.
34. On March 31, 2026, Claimant attended a telehealth appointment with Dr.
McLaughlin. At that time, Dr. McLaughlin discussed Dr. Grigg’s surgical
recommendation with Claimant. It was noted that Claimant wished to undergo the
recommended surgery. Dr. McLaughlin also noted that he had reviewed Dr. Cebrian’s
IME report. Dr. McLaughlin stated his agreement with Dr. Griggs’s opinion that Claimant
8

suffered an acute injury. Dr. McLaughlin specifically described Claimant’s mechanism of
injury as “the cart got stuck and she required a coworker to move it. And she was pulling
and trying to pull a cart and yanked very hard to pull it out as well as to push it forward
and that is what led to the acute right elbow injury.”
35. Dr. Cebrian’s hearing testimony was consistent with his written reports. Dr.
Cebrian reiterated his opinion that based upon his review of Claimant’s medical records,
she did not suffer an acute injury. Dr. Cebrian points to the September 2023 Kaiser
records in which the term “atraumatic” was used, and there was no discussion of a cart
incident. Dr. Cebrian further testified that Claimant’s alleged injury should have been
reviewed pursuant to the occupational disease guidelines. It continues to be Dr.
Cebrian’s opinion that when such a causation analysis is done, Claimant’s work duties
do not have primary or secondary factors that would support an occupational exposure
or repetitive motion type injury.
36. Claimant testified that she wishes to undergo the surgery recommended
by Dr. Griggs. Claimant described her current symptoms as pain in her right arm from
her elbow down into her palm. Claimant also testified that she is unable to utilize her
right hand for her activities of daily living, including showering, cleaning, and cooking.
As of the date of the hearing, Claimant continues to be on modified duty.
37. Respondents wish to withdraw their admission in this claim. As a result,
Respondents are effectively contesting the compensability of Claimant’s work injury.
38. The ALJ finds Claimant’s hearing testimony to be credible and persuasive.
The ALJ specifically credits Claimant’s testimony regarding the September 2023 cart
and elevator incident and the immediate onset of her right elbow symptoms. The
Claimant’s description of that incident has remained unchanged since she reported the
incident to Employer. The failure of the Kaiser providers to accurately record the
mechanism of injury does not negate the credibility of Claimant’s testimony and the
other medical records.
9

39. The ALJ also finds that it is clear from the medical records that Claimant’s
date of injury was in September 2023. The date of November 13, 2023, was entered on
the initial workers’ compensation paperwork due to Claimant’s reasonable
misunderstanding of the process. It was this November 13, 2023 date that was then
adopted as Claimant’s “date of injury”. This date has been continually used in this claim,
despite the clear indications in the medical records that Claimant was injured in
September3 2023.
40. The ALJ credits the opinions of Drs. Delarosa, McLaughlin, and Griggs
over the contrary opinions of Dr. Cebrian. The ALJ finds that Respondents have failed to
overcome the opinions of the DIME physician, Dr. Delarosa, by clear and convincing
evidence. The ALJ is not persuaded by Dr. Cebrian’s testimony that Claimant’s
condition should be evaluated under a repetitive motion or occupational disease
causation analysis. As noted above, the ALJ finds that Claimant’s credible testimony
demonstrates that she suffered an acute injury while employed with Employer.
Conclusions of Law
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado is to assure
the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical benefits to injured workers at a
reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of any litigation. Section 8-40-
102(1), C.R.S. A claimant in a Workers’ Compensation claim has the burden of proving
entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. Section 8-43-201, C.R.S.
A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering
all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probable than not. Page v. Clark, 197
Colo. 306, 592 P.2d 792 (1979). The facts in a Workers’ Compensation case are not
interpreted liberally in favor of either the rights of the injured worker or the rights of the
3 See the September 30, 2023 record in which NP Akbani noted “[o]going for the last
month, possibly longer”; and the November 15, 2023 report of Dr. Dimatteo that
references two months of symptoms.
10

employer. Section 8-43-201, supra. A Workers’ Compensation case is decided on its
merits. Section 8-43-201, supra.
B. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness’s testimony and actions; the
reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the testimony and
action; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has been contradicted; and
bias, prejudice, or interest. See Prudential Insurance Co. v. Cline, 98 Colo. 275, 57 P.2d
1205 (1936); CJI, Civil 3:16.
C. The ALJ’s factual findings concern only evidence that is dispositive of the
issues involved. The ALJ has not addressed every piece of evidence that might lead to
a conflicting conclusion and has rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as
unpersuasive. Magnetic Engineering, Inc. v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385
(Colo. App. 2000).
D. Section 8-42-107(8)(b)(III) and (c), C.R.S. provides that the DIME
physician’s finding of MMI and permanent medical impairment is binding unless
overcome by clear and convincing evidence. Clear and convincing evidence is highly
probable and free from substantial doubt, and the party challenging the DIME
physician’s finding must produce evidence showing it is highly probable that the DIME
physician is incorrect. Metro Moving & Storage Co. v. Gussert, 914 P.2d 411 (Colo.
App. 1995). A fact or proposition has been proved by clear and convincing evidence if,
considering all of the evidence, the trier-of-fact finds it to be highly probable and free
from substantial doubt. Metro Moving & Storage, supra. A mere difference of opinion
between physicians fails to constitute error. See Gonzales v. Browning Ferris Industries
of Colorado, W.C. No. 4-350-356 (March 22, 2000). The ALJ may consider a variety of
factors in determining whether a DIME physician erred in their opinions including
whether the DIME appropriately utilized the Medical Treatment Guidelines and the AMA
Guides in their opinions.
E. As found, Respondents have failed to overcome, by clear and convincing
evidence, the opinions of Dr. Delarosa regarding MMI. As found, Dr. Delarosa’s
11

opinions are supported by the medical records and shared by Drs. McLaughlin and
Griggs. Respondents have failed to establish anything other than a difference of opinion
between Dr. Delarosa and Dr. Cebrian. As found, the medical records and the opinions
of Drs. Delarosa, McLaughlin, and Griggs are credible and persuasive.
F. When the respondents attempt to modify an issue that previously has
been determined by an admission, they bear the burden of proof for the modification.
Section 8-43-201(1), C.R.S.; see also Salisbury v. Prowers County School District, W.C.
No. 4-702-144 (ICAO, June 5, 2012); Barker v. Poudre School District, W.C. No. 4-750-
735 (ICAO, July 8, 2011). Section 8-43-201(1), C.R.S., provides, in pertinent part, that
“a party seeking to modify an issue determined by a general or final admission, a
summary order, or a full order shall bear the burden of proof for any such modification.”
The amendment to Section 8-43-201(1), C.R.S. placed the burden on the respondents
and made a withdrawal the procedural equivalent of a reopening. Dunn v. St. Mary
Corwin Hospital, W.C. No. 4-754-838-01 (ICAO, Oct. 1, 2013).
G. As noted above, here Respondents’ attempt to withdraw their GAL
becomes an analysis of the compensability of the previously admitted June 13, 2018
injury. Therefore, the ALJ considers whether Claimant suffered an injury arising out of
and in the course and scope of her employment with the Employer.
H. A compensable industrial accident is one that results in an injury requiring
medical treatment or causing disability. The existence of a preexisting medical
condition does not preclude the employee from suffering a compensable injury where
the industrial aggravation is the proximate cause of the disability or need for treatment.
See H & H Warehouse v. Vicory, 805 P.2d 1167 (Colo. App. 1990); see also
Subsequent Injury Fund v. Thompson, 793 P.2d 576 (Colo. App. 1990). A work-related
injury is compensable if it “aggravates accelerates or combines with a preexisting
disease or infirmity to produce disability or need for treatment.” See H & H Warehouse
v. Vicory, supra.
I. As found, Respondents have failed to demonstrate, by a preponderance
of the evidence, that they should be permitted to withdraw their admission of liability in
12

this case. As found, Claimant suffered an injury that arose out of and in the course and
scope of her employment with employer. As found, Claimant’s testimony, the medical
records, and the opinions of Drs. Delarosa, McLaughlin, and Griggs are credible and
persuasive on this issue.
Order
It is therefore ordered:
1. Claimant suffered a compensable injury to her right elbow.
2. Respondents’ request to withdraw the General Admission of Liability is
denied and dismissed.
3. Respondents have failed to overcome the opinions of the DIME physician.
4. All matters not determined here are reserved for future determination.
Dated June 1, 2026.
Cassandra M. Sidanycz
Administrative Law Judge
Office of Administrative Courts

You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as long as the certificate of mailing
attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it within twenty (20) days after
13

mailing or service of the order of the ALJ; and (2) That you mailed it to the above

title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-276-754-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-276-754-001
Issues
Whether Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that
⮚
she is entitled to an award of temporary total disability (“TTD”) benefits for the period of
May 14, 2025 through ongoing?
Prior to the hearing, the parties stipulated to an average weekly wage
⮚
(“AWW”) of $1,751.27.
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant sustained an admitted injury arising out of and in the course and
scope of her employment on Jun 13, 2024 when she was involved in a motor vehicle
accident while driving a bus for Employer in Baggs, Wyoming. Claimant sustained
injuries to her neck, back, head and lower right leg.
2. Following Claimant’s injury, Claimant came under the care of Work
Partners Occupational Health. Claimant was initially provided with work restrictions but
was released to return to work without restrictions as of July 24, 2024. Claimant
testified that when she was on work restrictions she was performing office work.
3. After Claimant was released to return to work without restrictions, she
returned to her previous position driving a bus for Employer. Claimant testified that this
position provided her with a split shift where she would operate the bus to drop off
employees at a job site, then do other tasks, before operating the bus again to pick up
the employees from the job site. Claimant testified that while she could perform this
work which involved driving for a few hours before getting a break.
1

4. Claimant testified at hearing that she was furloughed from her
employment effective February 26, 2025. Claimant testified she was instructed to apply
for “job attached” unemployment benefits (which she did apply for and received) as
there was the possibility that Claimant would be rehired by Employer. Claimant testified
she was subsequently terminated on April 22, 2025.
5. Claimant continued to treat with Work Partners and on May 14, 2025,
Claimant was provided with new work restrictions that included no more than three
consecutive hours of driving at a time. Claimant testified at hearing that due to the work
restrictions, Claimant is not able to complete her Class B training for a commercial
drivers’ license.
6. Claimant was provided with new work restrictions on December 9, 2025
that included no more than 3 hours walking per day, 2 hours standing, and 3 hours
sitting per day. Claimant’s restrictions include alternating between standing and sitting.
7. Ms. Brown testified at hearing that she has not returned to work in any
capacity since being laid off by Employer.
8. Employer presented the testimony of Brian Campbell, the Human
Resources (“HR”) Manager for Employer at hearing. Mr. Campbell confirmed Claimant
was injured while working in her position as a crew bus driver. Mr. Campbell noted that
in Claimant’s position with Employer, her work duties included transporting the crews
from the hotel or district office to the work site locations. Mr. Campbell testified that in
addition to these job duties, a crew bus driver may also need to drive the vehicles to
pick up parts for Employer, if necessary. Claimant would also be required to clean the
buses as part of her work duties.
9. Mr. Campbell testified Claimant was released to return to work without
restrictions, but was then furloughed in February 2025. Mr. Campbell testified Claimant
was furloughed as part of a reduction in work force and that while Employer had hoped
to be able to bring people back, Employer was ultimately unable to do so and
approximately 10-12 people were separated from employment with Employer, including
Claimant.
2

10. Mr. Campbell testified that after Claimant was let go, she has not
contacted Employer about being rehired.
11. The ALJ credits Claimant’s testimony at hearing along with the medical
records entered into evidence at hearing and finds that Claimant has established that it
is more probable than not that she is entitled to an award of temporary total disability
benefits beginning May 14, 2025 and continuing until terminated by law. The ALJ
credits the medical records and finds that Claimant has established that as of May 14,
2025 Claimant was provided with work restrictions which constitute a disability for
Claimant that is related to her admitted work injury. The ALJ further credits Claimant’s
testimony at hearing and finds that Claimant was able to work for Employer based on
the split shift she was capable of performing, but has not been able to find employment
within her work restrictions. Therefore, Claimant is entitled to an award of temporary
disability benefits commencing May 14, 2025 and continuing until terminated by law.
12. Claimant testified at hearing that she was involved in a motor vehicle
accident that was not related to her employment with Employer when she was in
Oklahoma on May 30, 2025. Claimant testified that as a result of the May 30, 2025
motor vehicle accident, she had chest wall contusions and injuries to her shins.
Claimant testified that she did not receive work restrictions for the May 30, 2025 motor
vehicle accident. The ALJ finds Claimant’s testimony regarding the May 30, 2025 motor
vehicle accident to be credible and persuasive and finds insufficient evidence presented
at hearing that would establish that the May 30, 2025 motor vehicle accident represents
an intervening event that would termination Claimant’s entitlement to TTD benefits.
Conclusions of Law
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101,
et seq., C.R.S. is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of
litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden of proving
entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-43-201, C.R.S. A
preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering all
3

of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 592
P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’ compensation case must be interpreted
neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of
respondents; and a workers’ compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-
201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law judge.
University Park Care Center v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637 (Colo. App.
2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a contrary inference, it
is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make credibility determinations, and
draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at 641. When determining credibility,
the fact finder should consider, among other things, the consistency or inconsistency of
the witness's testimony and actions; the reasonableness or unreasonableness
(probability or improbability) of the testimony and actions; the motives of the witness;
whether the testimony has been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential
Insurance Co. v. Cline, 57 P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Industrial Claim
Appeals Office, 183 P.3d 684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be
assigned expert testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v.
Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert
testimony is subject to conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by
crediting part or none of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Industrial
Commission, 441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to
be dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has rejected
evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
D. To prove entitlement to temporary total disability (TTD) benefits, claimant
must prove that the industrial injury caused a disability lasting more than three work
4

shifts, that he left work as a result of the disability, and that the disability resulted in an
actual wage loss. PDM Molding, Inc. v. Stanberg, 898 P.2d 542 (Colo. 1995). Section
8-42-103(1)(a), supra, requires claimant to establish a causal connection between a
work-related injury and a subsequent wage loss in order to obtain TTD benefits. PDM
Molding, Inc. v. Stanberg, supra. The term disability, connotes two elements: (1)
Medical incapacity evidenced by loss or restriction of bodily function; and (2)
Impairment of wage earning capacity as demonstrated by claimant's inability to resume
his prior work. Culver v. Ace Electric, 971 P.2d 641 (Colo. 1999). There is no statutory
requirement that claimant establish physical disability through a medical opinion of an
attending physician; claimant's testimony alone may be sufficient to establish a
temporary disability. Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952 P.2d 831 (Colo. App. 1997). The
impairment of earning capacity element of disability may be evidenced by a complete
inability to work, or by restrictions which impair the claimant's ability effectively and
properly to perform his regular employment. Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy & Co., 964 P.2d
595 (Colo.App. 1998).
E. As found, Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence
that she is entitled to an award of TTD commencing May 14, 2025 when she was
provided with work restrictions from her treating physicians that limited her driving ability
to shifts lasting no more than three hours. As found, the testimony of Claimant and
medical records entered into evidence present credible evidence that Claimant is
entitled to an award commencing May 14, 2025 and continuing until terminated by
statute or law.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Respondents shall pay Claimant TTD benefits based on the stipulated
AWW of $1,751.27 for the period of May 14, 2025 and continuing until terminated by
law or statute.
2. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
