6

Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. 5-294-708-001
Issues
Whether Claimant proved by a preponderance of the evidence that there existed
➢
a mistake, an error, a change of condition, or fraud warranting a reopening of her
workers’ compensation claim.
If Claimant proved that her claim should be reopened, then whether Claimant
➢
proved by a preponderance of the evidence that she is entitled to disfigurement
benefits.
If Claimant proved that her claim should be reopened, then whether Claimant
➢
proved by a preponderance of the evidence that she is entitled to additional
medical benefits.
If Claimant proved that her claim should be reopened, then whether Claimant
➢
proved by a preponderance of the evidence that she is entitled to permanent total
disability benefits.
If Claimant proved that her claim should be reopened, then whether Claimant
➢
proved by a preponderance of the evidence that the average weekly wage
admitted in the final admission of liability is incorrect.
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant, a 36-year-old female, was an employee whose right foot was injured
while working for Respondent on December 4, 2024.
2. Claimant presented initially to Dr. TwoBears on December 13, 2024, with a
complaint of right foot pain after a fellow employee pushed a roller onto her foot
at work. Claimant reported pain at 8/10. Dr. TwoBears diagnosed Claimant with a

right foot crush injury, ordered ibuprofen, and physical therapy. Dr. TwoBears
additionally ordered light-work duty with accompanying restrictions.
3. On December 18, 2024, Claimant presented to PA-C Skvarca. Claimant
maintained a pain level of 8/10. Claimant reported pain in the right foot-top and
heel; however, ibuprofen was helping. PA-C Skvarca evaluated Claimant’s foot
and noted no symptoms of compartment syndrome, no out-of-proportion pain, no
paresthesia, no pain with range of motion distal to the injury, no pallor
pulselessness, and no paralysis. PA-C Skvarca reviewed Claimant’s X-ray
impressions from her last visit: (1) no acute bony fracture, or joint subluxation or
dislocation; (2) no soft-tissue emphysema, radiodense soft tissue abnormality or
foreign body seen; (3) consider follow-up evaluation with MRI for further
assessment if symptoms persist or worsen.
4. On March 13, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman. Dr. Cheesman
ordered diclofenac sodium and an MRI of the right foot as well as additional
referral for durable medical equipment in addition to prior prescribed orders.
5. On April 10, 2025, Dr. Shinault conducted an MRI of Claimant’s right foot and
had the following impressions: (1) intact lateral ankle ligaments and syndesmotic
ligament complex; (2) intact deltoid ligament complex and spring ligament
complex; (3) intact peroneal, medial flexor, extensor, and Achilles tendons; (4) no
acute or occult fracture, osteochondral lesion along the talar dome, or evidence
of tarsal coalitions; (5) intact tarsal tunnel, sinus tarsi, and plantar fascia, no
significant muscular atrophy, nor signal alterations to suggest denervation-type
injury; and (6) no significant ankle joint effusion or distinct loose bodies in the
synovial space.
6. On April 16, 2025, Claimant presented to podiatrist Dr. Zyzda. Dr. Zyzda
reviewed the MRI, X-ray, and medical history and discussed with Claimant her
treatment options. Claimant reported continued pain and a slight limp. Dr. Zyzda
2

ordered gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime, orthotics, cortisone injection, and referral
for neurological consultation.
7. On April 30, 2025, Claimant presented for follow-up to Dr. Zyzda. Claimant self-
reported being 20% improved. Claimant noted she had an appointment with a
physiatrist the following day. Dr. Zyzda remarked that most of Claimant’s pain
appeared neurogenic given that the MRI and the X-ray were negative.
8. On May 1, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Aschberger for physiatrist review.
Claimant reported for the first time she had irritation proximally in the distal
foreleg and paresthesia distally at the toes. Dr. Aschberger increased Claimant’s
gabapentin to 300 mg three times daily for the next “couple of weeks.” Dr.
Aschberger noted possible plantar fasciitis in addition to the initial crush injury
diagnosis. Dr. Aschberger also ordered evaluation of Claimant’s foot to rule out
complex regional pain syndrome. He wrote in his report that he recommended
electrodiagnostic testing “to rule out neural compromise.” On the same day,
Claimant presented to Dr. Zyzda for fitting and ordered her back in three weeks
for orthotic fitting and neurological review.
9. On May 8, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman for follow-up occupational
care. Dr. Cheesman noted Claimant was “hyper emotional” and “extremely
charge[d]” resulting in a request for a chaperone for Claimant as Claimant was
“inconsolable.” Dr. Cheesman noted that he was unable to get coherent
information from Claimant as Claimant was attempting to explain while “crying
hysterically” and her attempts were “very convoluted.” Claimant expressed she
did not feel comfortable or safe going to the other Concentra clinic. Dr.
Cheesman noted that Claimant felt that she was slighted in some manner.
10. On May 23, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Muthiah Nachiappan at UC Health
for a Bone/Joint 3 Phase bone scan. Dr. Nachiappan’s impression was negative,
noting: (1) no significant abnormality or asymmetry in blood flow (radionuclide
3

angiography); (2) no significant abnormality or asymmetry in blood pool (soft
tissue); and (3) expected distribution of radiotracer on delayed phase imaging
(skeletal.)
11. On May 29, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Zyzda. Claimant reported orthotics
felt good on her left foot while wearing a surgical shoe for her right foot. Dr.
Zyzda noted Claimant was in no apparent distress and was alert and
cooperative. Claimant reported pain at 7/10, an improvement from earlier in May
when Claimant’s self-reported pain was 8/10.
12. On June 2, 2025, Claimant presented to UC Health for an EMG performed by Dr.
Dianna Quan. Dr. Quan’s findings noted, “this was [a] normal study. There was
no electrophysiologic evidence of a generalized polyneuropathy or focal
entrapment neuropathy affecting the symptomatic right lower limb at this time.”
13. On June 6, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman. Dr. Cheesman noted
that the EMG did not show any evidence of lower extremity involvement. Dr.
Cheesman noted Claimant appeared more comfortable with her orthotics and
they neither caused her pain nor discomfort in the right foot.
14. On June 11, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Zyzda for podiatrist follow-up.
Claimant noted she performed a three-phase bone scan and EMG at UC Health.
Claimant reported that the orthotics were not making much of a difference. On
evaluation, Dr. Zyzda noted, “She essentially has hypersensitivity and pain
everywhere I touch on the foot and ankle.” Dr. Zyzda noted there appeared only
to be neurogenic pain and discharged Claimant as she was at maximum medical
improvement (“MMI”) orthopedically with orders to follow up with Dr. Aschberger.
15. On June 18, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Aschberger. Dr. Aschberger noted
that Claimant was “quite angry” and reported numerous issues. First, Claimant
stated that the prescription for her gabapentin has been sent in incorrectly with
4

verification that two refills had been provided to Claimant. Claimant reported she
did not refill the medications. Dr. Aschberger verified the prescriptions were
correctly sent in and filled. Second, Claimant reported obtaining a three-phase
bone scan at UC Health. Dr. Aschberger noted this referral did not originate from
their office. Next, Dr. Aschberger reviewed Claimant’s three-phase bone scan
and noted it was negative for any findings by both him and UC Health. Dr.
Aschberger wrote, “I do not believe it is possible to establish a further working
relationship with [Claimant.]” Dr. Aschberger further wrote, “[Claimant] is
skeptical regarding testing results as performed, although this was performed at
UC Health, outside our facilities, and she has expressed skepticism regarding
recommendations.” Dr. Aschberger found Claimant’s symptoms were negative
for CRPS and the current examination, including three-phase bone scan by UC
Health. Dr. Aschberger maintained Gabapentin orders and opined with Dr.
Cheesman that a psychological assessment is warranted “to help determine
whether therapeutic relationship is possible and the appropriate approach.”
Claimant walked out of the appointment without scheduling any further
evaluations.
16. On July 9, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman for follow-up. Dr.
Cheesman noted Claimant appeared with a workup for CRPS inconsistent with
CRPS given the 3D bone scan and EMG. Dr. Cheesman observed that Claimant
was aggressively emotional and that he was unable to understand her at times
due to the outbursts of tears, flight of speech, and convoluted nature of speech.
Dr. Cheesman offered Claimant an interpreter, which Claimant declined.
Claimant stated she cannot function with activities of daily living and believes her
coworkers are upset with her due to her medication use and naps throughout the
day. Dr. Cheesman noted Dr. Aschberger recommended pain psychology;
however, there was an unclear source for the pain.
17. On August 6, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman. Dr. Cheesman did not
have a source for Claimant’s significant debilitation. Claimant requested a pill that
5

would make her feel better, noting that she did not want to take gabapentin any
longer due to how it made her sleepy. Dr. Cheesman advised Claimant that all
medications have some form of side effect and there was not a singular drug he
could prescribe that would fully alleviate Claimant’s symptomology. Dr.
Cheesman placed Claimant at MMI with no impairment rating.
18. On September 4, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman. Dr. Cheesman
documented that the referral for a second opinion to another physiatrist was
declined by the other physiatrist. Claimant presented somberly and refused to
communicate with Dr. Cheesman. Claimant requested an Ewe interpreter from
Ghana. Dr. Cheesman noted they were unable to get an interpreter with her
dialect that day as the phone interpreters spoke with a Togo dialect. Claimant
reported she did not wish to proceed without an interpreter present. Dr.
Cheesman noted Claimant has been offered an interpreter at prior appointments
and Claimant was only now raising the need for an interpreter. Dr. Cheesman
noted Claimant was at MMI from August 6, 2025, visit.
19. On September 30, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman. Dr. Cheesman
secured an interpreter that permitted Claimant to speak in a mixture of English
and Ewe. Dr. Cheesman noted that Claimant was okay with proceeding forward
with the mixed interpretations. Dr. Cheesman discussed the lack of objective
findings and the lack of any localization for the pain she reports with multiple
diagnostics. Claimant reported that someone had told her that there were
abnormalities with her nerves; however, Dr. Cheesman observed that all nerve
diagnostics were negative. Dr. Cheesman noted Claimant remained at MMI. Dr.
Cheesman had released Claimant to full duty on that date without restrictions
and without any permanent impairment. Dr. Cheesman noted that Claimant
reached MMI on August 06, 2025.
20. On October 2, 2025, Respondents filed its Final Admission of Liability
documenting medical benefits paid as $7,043.76, TTD totaling $2,044.96, TPD
6

totaling $4,003.69, no impairment rating or PPD, and no maintenance medical
care. Respondents asserted an overpayment of $1,666.67.
21. The Court notes an absence of credible evidence in the record that Claimant
challenged the October 2, 2025 FAL within thirty days by requesting a hearing or
a DIME. The Court therefore finds that the claim closed on the October 2, 2025
FAL.
22. Dr. Leland at UC Health noted in his report on August 28, 2025:
“I saw and evaluated the patient. I discussed the case with Dr. Rakowski
and agree with the findings [and] plan as documented. Patient does not
have any evidence of any structural abnormalities in her right foot
following her crush injury. That being said, she does have some nerve
hypersensitivity and concern over development of complex regional pain
syndrome. It was recommended that a pain management referral be
obtained. Additionally, to ensure that there is no evidence of any structural
damage, an MRI was ordered.”
23. Dr. Leland did not make any note of Claimant’s prior medical imaging.
24. On October 19, 2025, Claimant presented for an MRI of her right foot. Dr.
Leland’s impression was negative for any evidence of structural abnormalities.
He recommended that Claimant progress in her activity as tolerated. Dr. Leland
specifically wrote, “In light of the fact that her symptoms have resolved and her
MRI shows no evidence of any structural abnormalities, continued nonoperative
treatment course is recommended.” Dr. Leland did not recommend any curative
medical treatment.
25. However, even Dr. Leland noted Claimant was negative for any indicators and
discharged Claimant on October 23, 2025. Dr. Leland also documented that
7

Claimant’s self-reported symptoms had resolved and that the dorsal foot swelling
was resolving. Dr. Leland’s orders included follow-up as needed with activity to
progress as she could tolerate.
26. Claimant testified at hearing on her own behalf.
27. Claimant testified that she had accepted a twelve-week position with Employer
and had signed on to begin working full time at a rate of $20.77 per hour prior to
her injury.
28. Claimant testified that after her injury, she went to Concentra for tetanus shots
and was experiencing leg pain. She testified that she subsequently treated with
different doctors and was placed on temporary restrictions. According to
Claimant, her employer threatened to fire her while she was subject to those
restrictions.
29. Claimant testified that her podiatrist, Dr. Zyzda, diagnosed her with plantar
fasciitis and prescribed gabapentin to help her sleep. Claimant further testified
that physical therapists noted she had achieved only 25% of her pre-injury
capacity by February 2025.
30. Claimant testified that the MRI she underwent examined only her ankle, not her
foot, and that she was unable to keep her leg straight during the MRI.
31. Claimant testified that she was required to use an interpreter during the
September 30 medical examination.
32. Claimant testified that, at the time she was placed at maximum medical
improvement (MMI), she continued to have restrictions imposed by Dr.
Cheesman. Claimant testified that the existence of those restrictions was not
documented in Dr. Cheesman's report, which she contended evidenced fraud or
8

error. Based on this contention, Claimant testified that her claim should not have
been closed.
33. Claimant testified that she decided in December to seek reopening of her claim
because her condition was “still ongoing.” She further testified that the claim
should not have been closed while referrals remained pending, including referrals
to a spine specialist and a psychiatrist at UC Health. Additionally, she testified
that her prior attorney did not communicate with her regarding the closure of her
claim, resulting in her missing the deadline to object to the final admission of
liability.
34. Claimant testified regarding the May 1, 2025 report of Dr. Aschberger.
Specifically, she testified that Dr. Aschberger's recommendation for
electrodiagnostic testing “to rule out neural compromise” demonstrated that he
was predisposed to find no neural compromise. Claimant's testimony suggested
that she believed Dr. Aschberger had prejudged her condition.
35. Claimant testified that she later sought treatment in an emergency room after the
claim was closed and that she was homeless at that time.
36. With respect to disfigurement, Claimant testified that the right corner of her foot
had edema and that her toes were not in the proper position.
37. The Court finds Claimant’s testimony only partially credible. The Court does not
doubt that Claimant sustained a compensable right-foot injury on December 13,
2024, and experienced pain and discomfort thereafter. However, the severity and
persistence of the symptoms and limitations described at hearing are not fully
supported by the greater weight of the evidence. Throughout the course of
treatment, multiple objective diagnostic studies—including X-rays, an MRI, a
three-phase bone scan, and EMG testing—failed to identify a structural,
neurological, or other objective basis for the degree of impairment alleged by
9

Claimant. Treating providers repeatedly documented normal or negative findings,
ruled out complex regional pain syndrome, and ultimately placed Claimant at
maximum medical improvement without permanent impairment. The Court
further notes that several providers documented difficulties in obtaining coherent
information from Claimant, observed significant emotional responses
disproportionate to examination findings, and recorded Claimant’s skepticism
regarding negative diagnostic results and medical recommendations. Claimant’s
hearing testimony was also inconsistent with portions of the medical record,
including her assertion that the MRI did not evaluate her foot and her contention
that undisclosed restrictions remained in place at the time of MMI despite the
contemporaneous medical records reflecting otherwise. While the Court credits
Claimant’s subjective reports of ongoing pain and acknowledges her sincere
belief that she remained symptomatic, the Court affords greater weight to the
objective medical evidence and the opinions of the treating physicians.
Accordingly, the Court finds that Claimant’s testimony is credible only to the
extent it establishes the occurrence of the work injury and some resulting
symptoms, but not to the extent it alleges ongoing disabling impairment,
entitlement to additional benefits, or error in the closure of the claim.
38. The Court finds that Claimant has not proved by a preponderance of the
evidence that there existed a change of condition warranting reopening.
Following closure of the claim on October 2, 2025, the records documented
continued complaints of pain but did not show any worsening of Claimant’s
condition. To the contrary, the post-closure medical evidence is consistent with
the findings that existed at the time of maximum medical improvement. Dr.
Leland’s evaluation and subsequent MRI failed to identify any structural
abnormality of the right foot and did not result in any recommendation for curative
treatment. Rather, Dr. Leland documented that Claimant’s symptoms had
resolved, noted improvement in the previously reported swelling, recommended
only progression of activity as tolerated, and discharged Claimant from care on
an as-needed basis. The Court further finds that Claimant’s disagreement with
10

the opinions of the authorized treating physicians, her belief that additional
referrals should have been pursued, and her continued subjective complaints of
pain are insufficient to lead the Court to a contrary finding.
39. The Court finds that Claimant has not proved by a preponderance of the
evidence that there existed a mistake or error warranting reopening in this case.
The claim in this matter was closed not as the result of any factual or legal
mistake, but as the result of Respondents’ October 2, 2025 Final Admission of
Liability becoming final after Claimant failed to timely contest it within thirty days.
The Court finds that Respondents filed a Final Admission of Liability on October
2, 2025, based upon the opinions of the authorized treating physicians that
Claimant had reached maximum medical improvement without permanent
impairment and without the need for additional curative treatment. Those
opinions were supported by extensive diagnostic testing, including X-rays, MRI
imaging, a three-phase bone scan, and EMG studies, all of which were
essentially negative for objective findings explaining the level of impairment
alleged by Claimant. Although Claimant contends that the claim should not have
closed because additional referrals remained pending, because she disagreed
with the opinions of the treating physicians, because she believes the MRI was
inadequate, and because she did not timely challenge the Final Admission of
Liability due to a lack of communication with her former attorney, those
circumstances do not establish a mistake or error underlying the closure of the
claim which would warrant reopening the claim in the Court’s view. The Court
further finds no persuasive evidence that Dr. Cheesman incorrectly placed
Claimant at maximum medical improvement, failed to document material
restrictions that actually existed, or otherwise made a mistake that would justify
reopening. At most, the evidence demonstrates Claimant's disagreement with the
medical conclusions reached by the authorized providers and her dissatisfaction
with the closure of the claim.
11

40. The Court finds that Claimant has not proved by a preponderance of the
evidence that there exists fraud in this case warranting a reopening. Although
Claimant suggested that fraud occurred because Dr. Cheesman allegedly failed
to document continuing work restrictions at the time he placed her at maximum
medical improvement, the record contains no evidence persuasively supporting
that allegation. The Court finds no credible evidence that any physician,
employer, insurer, or other participant in the claim knowingly misrepresented
material facts, concealed relevant information, falsified medical records, or
otherwise engaged in deceptive conduct. Rather, the evidence demonstrates that
Claimant received extensive medical evaluation and diagnostic testing from
multiple providers over an extended period of time. The conclusions reached by
those providers were generally consistent in finding an absence of objective
abnormalities sufficient to support ongoing impairment, permanent restrictions, or
additional curative treatment. Claimant’s dissatisfaction with those conclusions
and her belief that the providers were mistaken, biased, or should have pursued
additional testing do not establish fraud. Nor does the fact that Claimant
disagrees with the determination that she reached maximum medical
improvement constitute evidence of fraudulent conduct.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S., is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
12

the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceeding is the exclusive domain of the administrative law judge.
University Park Care Center v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637 (Colo.
App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a contrary
inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make credibility
determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at 641. When
determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other things, the
consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions; the
reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has been
contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Insurance Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert testimony
is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off.,
55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is subject to
conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting part or none
of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Industrial Commission, 441 P.2d
21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Engineering, Inc. v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App.
2000).
Reopening
D. Once a claim is closed, it may be reopened only on grounds of fraud,
overpayment, error, mistake, or change in condition. Section 8-43-303, C.R.S.
A “change in condition” refers to a “change in the condition of the original
13

compensable injury or to a change in claimant’s physical or mental condition
which can be causally connected to the original compensable injury.” Cordova 55
P.3d 186 at 189; In re Caraveo, W.C. No. 4-358-465 (October 25, 2006).
Reopening is appropriate when the claimant’s degree of permanent disability has
changed since MMI or where the claimant is entitled to additional medical or
temporary disability benefits that are causally connected to the compensable
injury. See Duarte v. Glen Ayr Health Center, W.C. No. 4-521-453 (June 8,
2007).
E. In cases of allegation of a change in condition, the claimant bears the burden of
proof to establish, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the worsening of
their physical or mental condition is causally related to the industrial injury.
Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952 P.2d 831 (Colo. App. 1997); Savio House v.
Dennis, 665 P.2d 141 (Colo. App. 1983). However, a change of condition by itself
is not sufficient to justify reopening, and the claimant must also establish that
reopening is appropriate because the claimant’s degree of permanent disability
has changed, or when additional medical or temporary disability benefits are
warranted. Richards v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 996 P.2d 756, 758 (Colo. App.
2000).
F. Reopening may be granted based on any mistake of fact that calls into question
the propriety of a prior award. Kehler v. Labor Etc Inc, W.C. No. 5-000-017 at *3
(Jan. 6, 2023). In determining whether a particular mistake of fact or law justifies
reopening, the ALJ may consider whether the mistake could have been avoided
if the party seeking reopening timely exercised procedural or appellate rights
prior to entry of the award. Klosterman v. Indus. Comm’n, 694 P.2d 873 (Colo.
App. 1984); Webster v. Czarnowski Display Service Inc, W.C. No. 5-009-761-014
at *6 (Nov. 16, 2022).
G. The reopening authority granted to ALJs by § 8-43-303 “is permissive, and
whether to reopen a prior award when the statutory criteria have been met is left
to the sound discretion of the ALJ.” Cordova, 55 P.3d at 189.
H. The Court concludes, as found, that Claimant has not proved by a
preponderance of the evidence that reopening is warranted on the bases of
14

mistake, error, change of condition, or fraud. The claim closed by operation of
law when Claimant did not timely contest the October 2, 2025 Final Admission of
Liability through a request for hearing or a DIME. Claimant has not proved the
existence of any factual or legal mistake underlying the closure of the claim that
would warrant reopening, nor has she proved fraud by any physician, employer,
insurer, or other participant. To the contrary, the evidence is that Claimant
received extensive evaluation from multiple providers, including X-rays, MRI
imaging, a three-phase bone scan, and EMG testing, none of which identified
objective findings supporting ongoing disability, permanent impairment, or the
need for additional curative treatment. The Court also notes the post-closure
medical evidence, which is consistent with, rather than contrary to, the opinions
upon which the claim was closed. Although the Court finds that Claimant
sincerely believes she remained symptomatic and disagrees with the conclusions
of the authorized treating physicians, disagreement with medical opinions,
dissatisfaction with claim closure, or the existence of unresolved subjective
complaints does not warrant the Court exercising discretion to reopen Claimant’s
claim. Accordingly, the Court declines to exercise its discretionary authority to
reopen the claim and concludes that Claimant’s request for reopening must be
denied.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant has not proved by a preponderance of the evidence
that there exists mistake, error, change in condition, or fraud
warranting reopening of her claim.
15

2. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future
determination.
If you are dissatisfied with the Judge's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on certificate of mailing or service; otherwise,
the Judge's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as long as the
certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it within twenty
(20) days after mailing or service of the order of the Judge; and (2) That you mailed it to
the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. For statutory reference,
see section 8-43-301(2), C.R.S. For further information regarding procedures to follow
when filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may access a petition to
review form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.

Findings of Fact
1. Claimant worked for Respondents as a laborer. On February 28, 2025, Claimant
was working for Employer when he walked through a restricted area where a
coworker was operating backhoe and was struck on the torso by the bucket of
the backhoe. Claimant reported the incident to his supervisor and was sent to
Concentra for evaluation.
2. On February 28, 2025, Claimant presented to Concentra where he was
evaluated by Keith Meier, NP. Claimant reported he was struck on the left side of
his back by the bucket of a backhoe, and that he “just had a little discomfort.” NP
Meier conducted a physical examination of Claimant’s cervical and thoracic
spine, which showed normal range of motion and no tenderness or pain. He
diagnosed Claimant with a thoracic wall contusion and prescribed no treatment
or medication. NP Meier indicated that physical therapy and prescription
medication were considered but not prescribed because Claimant had minimal
1

loss of function and over the counter medications would be sufficient. Claimant
was then discharged at maximum medical improvement, with no restrictions or
impairment. NP Meier’s report was co-signed by Kathryn Bird, D.O. The WC 164
form associated with the visit was signed by Lori Long-Miller, M.D., and placed
Claimant at MMI effective February 28, 2025, with no impairment, and no work
restrictions.
3. At some point after February 28, 2025, Employer terminated Claimant’s
employment for violating safety protocols resulting in the incident.
4. Between March 12, 2025 and March 20, 2025, Claimant was seen at Kaiser
Permanente’s urology clinic. The Kaiser record from March 12, 2025 includes an
“Active Problem List” which identifies several non-urology related concerns, such
as hearing loss, rhinitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease and chronic cough, but
does not include any issues related to Claimant’s back or thoracic spine.
5. On March 14, 2025, Employer filed a First Report of Injury, indicating Claimant
reported the incident on February 28, 2025, and that he sustained a strain to the
upper back area.
6. On April 4, 2025, Claimant filed a Worker’s Claim for Compensation with the
Division, alleging that he sustained a lumbar strain on February 28, 2025.
7. On April 24, 2025, Respondents filed a Final Admission of Liability (FAL) which
indicated an MMI date of February 28, 2025, and denied liability for medical
treatment after MMI,
8. On May 19, 2025, Claimant objected to the FAL and initiated the DIME Process.
9. On May 30, 2025, Claimant filed an Application for Indigent Determination,
requesting that Respondents pay the costs of the DIME. On June 11, 2025, a
Prehearing Administrative Law Judge found Claimant indigent, thus requiring
Respondents to initially pay the DIME costs.
10. On August 15, 2025, Respondents conducted video surveillance of Claimant.
The video, which is approximately two-hours in length and taken over a period of
approximately four hours, shows Claimant engaging in physical labor, working on
2

what appears to be a drainage or irrigation project. Claimant can be seen walking
without difficulty; standing in the bucket of a moving backhoe; working with
various tools and materials, including a digging with a shovel, moving earth with
a pickaxe, trimming bushes with a hedge trimmer, using a wheel barrow;;
dumping a five-gallon bucket full of debris into a dumpster; and carrying,
dragging, and throwing without apparent difficulty numerous pieces of PVC
piping of various sizes (which appear to range in diameter from three to ten
inches, and at least 8 feet in length). Throughout the video, Claimant can be
seen walking, bending, squatting, carrying materials, and climbing a fence, all
without observable difficulty.
11. On September 4, 2026, Respondents submitted the video surveillance video to
Albert Hattem, M.D., for review. Dr. Hattem accurately described the Claimant’s
activity depicted and concluded that Claimant was properly placed at MMI on
February 28, 2025. He opined that Claimant was “not only fully recovered from
the effects of the 02/28/2025 work injury, but is remarkably agile, strong and fit
for a 60-year-old male. He further opined that Claimant was capable of working
fully unrestricted duty without the need for further care or work restrictions.
12. On September 26, 2025, Claimant underwent a DIME examination performed by
Bradley Abrahamson, M.D. After issuing an initial report, Dr. Abrahamson issued
an amended report on October 3, 2025, which contains his ultimate opinions.
The only records Dr. Abrahamson reviewed were Claimant’s February 28, 2025
visit at Concentra, and Dr. Hattem’s September 4, 2025 report. Claimant reported
to Dr. Abrahamson that when he was struck by the backhoe, he was thrown five
feet and lost consciousness. Claimant reported bilateral lumbar spine pain, hip
pain and pain radiating down his leg. Claimant also reported that he was unable
to work an 8 hour day, and that his friends told him he walked with a limp.
13. On examination, Dr. Abrahamson noted that Claimant’s left shoulder “lists
downwards causing a mild, nonspecific limp.” He noted no neurovascular
abnormalities, with the exception of light touch loss and tingling of the posterior
left leg but noted he could not determine that Claimant had any radiculopathy. He
3

noted that Claimant’s range of motion was “remarkably good.” Dr. Abrahamson
performed straight let testing and documented motion of 120 degrees on the right
and 117 on the left. He also performed lumbar range of motion measurements,
which showed a 2% impairment for lumbar flexion and 3% for lumbar extension,
with no other deficits. He assigned a provisional whole person impairment rating
of 10% for lumbar spine impairment, which included 5% for range of motion, and
5% for specific disorders under the AMA Guides table 53, II, B. He did not assign
an impairment for Claimant’s thoracic spine.
14. Dr. Abrahamson diagnosed Claimant with a thoracic contusion and determined
that Claimant had not reached MMI because he had “a host of residual
symptoms” and had not received treatment. He opined that Claimant could not
return to a labor job due to his ongoing symptoms but also noted that Claimant
did not require work restrictions. He recommended that receive at least two
months of physical therapy with care supervised by an authorized treating
provider.
15. On November 16, 2024, Claimant returned to Concentra, where he saw Melissa
Ginsburg, NP. Claimant reported back pain that improved after warming up and
cramping in his legs from back pain. NP Ginsburg noted that Claimant had
scoliosis which caused his right1 shoulder to be slightly higher than the left. She
reviewed the DIME report, and video surveillance, and indicated “Although I think
he is at MMI he may certainly benefit from PT and work conditioning.” On
examination, NP Ginsburg noted that Claimant had a loss of the normal thoracic
kyphosis and a round back deformity, tenderness in the left paraspinal area, and
full range of motion. Although Claimant reported pain with active range of motion.
She assessed Claimant as having a normal gait, and no muscular weakness. Her
1 NP Ginsburg’s record indicates “He does have scoliosis with the L shoulder slightly higher than
the left.” The ALJ infers that this is a typographical error, and that meant to indicate that the right
shoulder is higher than the left, which is consistent with Dr. Abrahamson’s findings.
4

diagnosis was a thoracic contusion, for which she prescribed physical therapy.
She imposed no work restrictions and indicated Claimant could work full duty.
16. On November 21, 2025, the parties conducted Dr. Abrahamson’s deposition. Dr.
Abrahamson testified that Claimant required physical therapy for his work injury
for spinal motion, stability, and strength. He indicated that physical therapy would
include assessments of mobility, and strength, and would help with Claimant’s
range of motion. He testified that during the DIME examination, Claimant “wasn’t
moving well.” During the deposition, Dr. Abrahamson viewed portions of the
video surveillance and testified he believed that Claimant felt discomfort
performing the activities shown in the video surveillance, that Claimant labored at
times lifting objects, that he did not move like an uninjured person, and that
Claimant was protecting himself during several activities.
17. Throughout his deposition, Dr. Abrahamson’s analysis of Claimant’s movements
and activities was based on ascribing “cultural” characteristics to the Claimant
and speculating about his ability to perform certain tasks. For example, when
shown a portion of the video where Claimant climbed over a four-foot tall fence,
Dr. Abrahamson testified that Claimant “wouldn’t have given it a thought if he
were not injured. He would have just jumped up there.” When questioned about
the Claimant’s apparent lack of difficulty performing physical labor, Dr.
Abrahamson testified “This is an individual that my culture cannot fathom
because what he can endure is ten times, a hundred times more, and act like it is
no big deal.” He also testified that “these guys … can choose at the beginning of
the shift that they are going to ignore the pain the whole time and just pretend
like it is not there. And so without being in his body, I can’t tell you how much
pain he is in. But he is choosing to ignore it, yeah.” Dr. Abrahamson’s opinions
offered no credible basis for this testimony beyond his personal belief and
cultural stereotypes, rather than an objective, medically based opinion.
18. Ultimately, Dr. Abrahamson stated that his impression of the video surveillance
was that Claimant could perform high-level physical tasks for between sixty to
ninety minutes but could not work a full shift. Dr. Abrahamson’s opinion that
5

Claimant could not work a full work shift is based on Claimant’s report that he
would be unable to do so.
19. On November 28, 2025, Claimant saw Shantell TwoBears, M.D., at Concentra.
Dr. TwoBears noted that Claimant’s care had been delayed due to him having
prostate surgery in Mexico after the February 28, 2025 work incident. Claimant
reported left lower back and hip pain causing “cramps” down his leg at night. On
examination, Dr. TwoBears noted tenderness in the paraspinal area, and limited
range of motion in all planes, with no other significant findings. She also noted
that Claimant has scoliosis. She assessed Claimant with a thoracic wall
contusion.
20. Claimant began physical therapy on November 28, 2025, at Concentra. Although
Claimant reported to Dr. TwoBears that he was not working, he reported to
physical therapy on the same day that he had been working some. It was noted
that Claimant had limited “vertebral mobility and spring” throughout the thoracic
spine, and normal lumbar range of motion. Claimant attended six physical
therapy visits through December 16, 2025, with no noted change in his reported
symptoms.
21. On December 18, 2026, Claimant returned to NP Ginsburg at Concentra.
Claimant reported that he felt good when doing exercises, but his pain returned
after cooling down. NP Ginsburg observed that Claimant was able to change his
position easily despite reporting pain in his lower back. NP Ginsburg’s
examination of Claimant’s thoracic spine was normal. Claimant reported
tenderness and pain with active range of motion of the lumbosacral spine,
although he had full range of motion and strength. NP Ginsburg diagnosed
Claimant with a thoracic wall contusion, and lumbar strain, but offered no
explanation as to how Claimant’s lumbar strain diagnosis was related to the
workplace incident ten months earlier.
22. Claimant completed three additional physical therapy visits from December 18,
2025 through December 30, 2025, with no significant improvement in his
6

reported symptoms. Claimant reported that he continued to work “side jobs” but
nothing consistent.
23. Claimant’s last documented medical visit was on January 6, 2026, when he
returned to NP Ginsburg. At that visit, Claimant reported that he felt “about the
same,” and that he had an “ache” that hurt with cold weather. Claimant also
reported that he had not been working. NP Ginsburg found that Claimant was at
MMI effective January 6, 2026, with no impairment. Claimant was released to full
duty without the need for further care.
24. On December 15, 2025, Claimant saw Elizabeth Wilcox, M.D., for an
independent medical examination (IME) requested by Respondents. Dr. Willcox
issued a report dated December 18, 2025, and testified at hearing. Dr. Wilcox
opined that Dr. Abrahamson erred in attributing a lumbar impairment to
Claimant’s thoracic contusion and in determining that Claimant had not reached
MMI. Dr. Wilcox testified that Claimant’s February 28, 2025 visit to Concentra
was a “first-aid only” visit, which indicated that Claimant did not sustain an injury
that required treatment. Specifically, there were no signs of trauma or bruising
documented, and no objective evidence of injury. As such, she believed Claimant
reached MMI on February 28, 2025.
25. With respect to the Claimant’s impairment rating, she opined that Dr.
Abrahamson erred in attributing Claimant’s reported bilateral lumbar spine pain
and radiating pain to his thoracic contusion. She noted that although Dr.
Abrahamson assigned no lumbar spine diagnosis, he provided a lumbar spine
impairment rating. Moreover, she indicated that the several of the lumbar spine
ranges of motion Dr. Abrahamson obtained for Claimant’s straight leg tests (120
and 117 degrees), and lumbar flexion (145 degrees) are not physiologically
possible. Dr. Wilcox’ also opined that the Claimant’s lack of need for care after
Claimant’s initial visit supported the lack of a permanent impairment. Finally, she
indicated that she had reviewed the video surveillance of Claimant and opined
that the videos did not demonstrate any evidence that Claimant had sustained an
injury. Dr. Wilcox’s opinions and testimony are credible and persuasive.
7

Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S., is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law
judge. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637
(Colo. App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a
contrary inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make
credibility determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at
641. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions;
the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has
been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Ins. Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert
testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is
subject to conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting
8

part or none of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n,
441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
Overcoming DIME re: MMI
D. Respondents have established by clear and convincing evidence that the DIME
physician’s MMI opinion is incorrect.
E. MMI exists at the point in time when “any medically determinable physical or
mental impairment as a result of injury has become stable and when no further
treatment is reasonably expected to improve the condition.” § 8-40-201(11.5),
C.R.S. A DIME physician’s finding that a party has or has not reached MMI is
binding on the parties unless overcome by clear and convincing evidence. § 8-
42-107(8)(b)(III), C.R.S.; Magnetic Eng’g, Inc., supra.
F. “Clear and convincing evidence” is evidence that demonstrates that it is “highly
probable” the DIME physician's opinion is incorrect. Qual-Med, Inc. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Office, 961 P.2d 590, 592 (Colo. App. 1998); Lafont v. WellBridge,
W.C. No. 4-914-378-02 (ICAO June 25, 2015). In other words, to overcome a
DIME physician's opinion, “there must be evidence establishing that the DIME
physician's determination is incorrect, and this evidence must be unmistakable
and free from serious or substantial doubt.” Adams v. Sealy, Inc., W.C. No. 4-
476-254 (ICAO Oct. 4, 2001). The enhanced burden of proof reflects an
underlying assumption that the physician selected by an independent and
unbiased tribunal will provide a more reliable medical opinion. Qual-Med, supra.
G. The mere difference of medical opinion does not constitute clear and convincing
evidence to overcome the opinion of the DIME physician. Javalera v. Monte Vista
Head Start, Inc., W.C. Nos. 4-532-166 & 4-523-097 (ICAO July 19, 2004); see
Shultz v. Anheuser Busch, Inc., W.C. No. 4-380-560 (ICAO Nov. 17, 2000).
9

Rather it is the province of the ALJ to assess the weight to be assigned
conflicting medical opinions on the issue of MMI. Oates v. Vortex Indus., WC 4-
712-812 (ICAO Nov. 21, 2008); Licata v. Wholly Cannoli Café, W.C. No. 4-863-
323-04 (ICAO July 26, 2016).
H. MMI is primarily a medical determination involving diagnosis of the claimant’s
condition. Berg v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 128 P.3d 270 (Colo. App. 2005);
Monfort Transp. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 942 P.2d 1358 (Colo. App.
1997). A determination of MMI requires the DIME physician to assess, as a
matter of diagnosis, whether various components of the claimant’s medical
condition are causally related to the industrial injury. Martinez v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Office, 176 P.3d 826 (Colo. App. 2007); Powell v. Aurora Public
Schools, W.C. No. 4-974-718-03 (ICAO Mar. 15, 2017). A finding that the
claimant needs additional medical treatment to improve his injury-related medical
condition by reducing pain or improving function is inconsistent with a finding of
MMI. MGM Supply Co. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 62 P.3d 1001 (Colo. App.
2002); Reynolds v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 794 P.2d 1090 (Colo. App.
1990); Sotelo v. National By-Products, Inc., W.C. No. 4-320-606 (ICAO Mar. 2,
2000). Thus, a DIME physician’s findings concerning the diagnosis of a medical
condition, the cause of that condition, and the need for specific treatments or
diagnostic procedures to evaluate the condition are inherent elements of
determining MMI.
I. Respondents have established by clear and convincing evidence that the DIME
physician erred by finding Claimant had not reached MMI and required further
medical treatment. Dr. Abrahamson’s determination that Claimant was not at
MMI was based on Claimant’s subjective symptoms, rather than objective
medical evidence, and he offered no medically reasonable explanation for
attributing Claimant’s lumbar spine complaints to his thoracic contusion.
Similarly, his opinion that Claimant required treatment is based primarily on the
lack of treatment, rather than a need to treat a thoracic spine contusion that
occurred seven months earlier. The ALJ finds credible the opinions of Dr. Wilcox
and NP Meier, that Claimant sustained a chest wall contusion that did not require
10

medical attention beyond an initial evaluation, which did not result in further
evaluation, medication, or the need for treatment. The ALJ concludes that Dr.
Abrahamson erred in determining that Claimant had not reached MMI when he
conducted his DIME examination.
J. Once it is determined that a DIME physician’s opinion on MMI has been overcome,
the correct MMI date becomes a question of fact for the ALJ. In re Claim of York,
W.C. No. 4-837-612-04 (ICAO May 4, 2016). To the extent Claimant sustained a
compensable injury, the ALJ finds the date of MMI to be February 28, 2025. The
credible evidence establishes that there was no further treatment that was
reasonably expected to improve the Claimant’s chest wall contusion.
Overcoming DIME re: Impairment Rating
K. A DIME physician’s medical impairment rating may be overcome only by clear
and convincing evidence. Clear and convincing evidence is that quantum and
quality of evidence which renders a factual proposition highly probable and free
from serious or substantial doubt. Thus, the party challenging the DIME
physician's findings must produce evidence showing it highly probable the DIME
physician is incorrect. Metro Moving & Storage Co. v. Gussert, 914 P.2d 411
(Colo. App. 1995); Lafont v. WellBridge D/B/A Colorado Athletic Club W.C. No. 4-
914-378-02 (ICAO June 25, 2015).
L. As a matter of diagnosis, the assessment of permanent medical impairment
inherently requires the DIME physician to identify and evaluate all losses that
result from the injury. Mosley v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 78 P.3d 1150 (Colo.
App. 2003). Consequently, a DIME physician’s finding that a causal relationship
exists between an injury and a particular impairment must be overcome by clear
and convincing evidence. Qual-Med, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 961
P.2d 590 (Colo. App. 1998); Watier-Yerkman v. Da Vita, Inc. W.C. No. 4-882-
517-02 (ICAO Jan. 12, 2015). The rating physician’s determination concerning
the causes of impairment should include an assessment of data collected during
a clinical evaluation and the mere existence of impairment does not create a
presumption of contribution by a factor with which the impairment is often
11

associated. Wackenhut Corp. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 17 P.3d 202 (Colo.
App. 2000).
M. Respondents have also established by clear and convincing evidence that Dr.
Abrahamson erred by assigning Claimant a lumbar spine impairment of 10%.
Under the AMA Guides, a spinal impairment rating is appropriate for range of
motion only where an injured worker has a diagnosis under Table 53. Dr.
Abrahamson assigned Claimant a 5% lumbar impairment based on Table 53.II.B,
which requires a disc or other soft tissue lesion that is “Unoperated, with
medically documented injury and a minimum of six months of medically
documented pain and rigidity with or without muscle spasm associated with
none-to-minimal degenerative changes on structural tests.” Dr. Abrahamson
offered no credible evidence to support that Claimant had a medically
documented injury to either a lumbar disc or lumbar soft tissue or that he had six
months of medically documented pain and rigidity, and his only diagnoses was a
thoracic contusion. He offered no cogent explanation for assigning Claimant a
lumbar impairment for a thoracic spine contusion. The ALJ also finds persuasive
Dr. Wilcox’s testimony and report indicating that Dr. Abrahamson’s range of
motion and straight leg raise measurements were not performed correctly, further
supporting the conclusion that the impairment rating itself was performed
incorrectly.
N. Once an ALJ finds that the DIME physician’s rating has been overcome, the
claimant’s correct medical impairment rating becomes a question of fact for the
ALJ to determine based on a preponderance of the evidence. Garlets v.
Memorial Hosp., W.C. No. 4-336-566 (ICAO Sep. 5, 2001). Once the DIME is
overcome, the DIME’s opinion regarding impairment is not given any special
weight, and the ALJ is free to consider other medical evidence of the claimant’s
permanent impairment. Id.; Mosely v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 78 P.3d 1150
(Colo. App. 2003). “The only limitation is that the ALJ’s finding must be supported
by the record and consistent with the AMA Guides and other rating protocols.”
Serena v. Pueblo Belmont OP Co. LLC, W.C. No. 4-922-344-01 (ICAO Dec. 1,
2015).
12

O. Given that Claimant reached MMI on the date of the February 28, 2025 work
incident and did not require medical treatment beyond an initial evaluation, the
ALJ finds that Claimant sustained no permanent impairment as a result of the
workplace incident. The finding of no impairment is consistent with the opinions
of NP Meier, who initially saw Claimant, NP Ginsburg, and Dr. Wilcox. The DIME
physicians’ assignment of a lumbar impairment is not supported by the medical
records or his own examination.
Withdrawal Of General Admission Of Liability
P. By filing an admission of liability and admitting for benefits, Respondents’
“admitted that the claimant has sustained the burden of proving entitlement to
benefits.” City of Brighton v. Rodriguez, 318 P.3d 496 (Colo. 2014). If
Respondents seek to withdraw the admission of liability, they must prove by a
preponderance of the evidence that Claimant did not sustain an injury that arose
out of and occurred in the course and scope of employment. See Section 8-41-
201(1), C.R.S. (“a party seeking to modify an issue determined by a general or
final admission . . . shall bear the burden of proof for any such modification.”).
Q. The Workers’ Compensation Act distinguishes between the terms “accident” and
“injury.” The term “accident refers to an unexpected, unusual, or undesigned
occurrence. Section 8-40-201(1), C.R.S. However, an “injury” refers to the
physical trauma caused by the accident and is the result of an accident. City of
Boulder v. Payne, 426 P.2d 194 (1967). The mere fact that an accident occurs
does not rise to the level of compensability unless the accident results in an
injury. Leary v. Vail Resorts, Inc. W.C. No. 5-075-399-002 (ICAO, April 24, 2020).
A compensable industrial accident is one that results in an injury requiring
treatment or causing disability. H & H Warehouse v. Vicory, 805 P.2d 1167 (Colo.
App. 1990). The fact that medical treatment occurred does not require a finding
that medical treatment was required because of a work incident. Washburn v.
City Market, W.C. 5-109-470 (ICAO June 3, 2020).
R. Respondents have failed to establish grounds for withdrawal of the admission of
liability. Claimant’s February 28, 2025 work incident resulted in a diagnosed
thoracic contusion that reasonably required medical treatment in the form of an
13

initial examination to evaluate the extent of the injury and determine whether
additional treatment was required. Although Claimant did not receive subsequent
treatment and sustained no disability, the medical examination Claimant received
is compensable medical treatment. The fact that the injury did not result in
disability does not render the medical treatment non-compensable. Respondents
request to withdraw their admission of liability is denied.
Repayment of DIME Expenses
S. Respondents have failed to establish grounds for requiring Claimant to repay
amounts Respondents paid for the DIME examination based on allegedly
fraudulent representation of income.
T. Claimant submitted his Application for Indigent Determination on May 30, 2025,
indicating Claimant earned no income. Respondents have offered no credible
evidence demonstrating Claimant’s income or earnings when the Application was
submitted on May 30, 2025, or showing that Claimant’s income exceeded the
indigent guidelines. Consequently, Respondents have failed to establish grounds
for requiring Claimant to repay Respondents the DIME fee.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Respondents have established by clear and convincing evidence that the DIME
physician’s opinion that Claimant has not reached maximum medical
improvement was incorrect, and that the DIME physician’s provisional
impairment rating was incorrect. Claimant reached maximum medical
improvement on February 28, 2025, with no permanent impairment.
2. Respondents’ request to withdraw their admission of liability is denied.
3. Respondents’ request for repayment of DIME fees is denied.
4. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.

Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-324-080-001
Issues
1. Whether Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence
that she suffered a compensable right shoulder injury during the course and scope of
employment with Employer on July 19, 2025.
2. Whether Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that
she is entitled to receive reasonable and necessary medical benefits that are causally
related to her July 19, 2025 right shoulder injury.
Procedural Matter
On May 28, 2026 Claimant filed the following two motions: (1) an Opposed
Motion for Extension of Time to File Proposed Findings of Fact; and (2) an Opposed
Motion to Reopen the Evidentiary Record. The motions are predicated on Claimant’s
May 19, 2026 diagnostic imaging including a Cervical Spine MRI and a Brachial Plexus
MRI. Claimant asserts the preceding reports contain critical, objective anatomical
findings that were not available at the time of the May 14, 2026 hearing. She promptly
provided the reports to Respondents’ counsel upon receipt on May 26, 2026. Claimant
contends that there is good cause for the reopening of the record to admit the reports
because their consideration “is necessary to ensure a complete medical record and to
prevent manifest injustice, as the findings directly correlate to the Claimant’s
documented impairment and determination of medical benefits.”
Despite Claimant’s arguments, she has failed to demonstrate good cause to
reopen the evidentiary record or extend the due date for filing position statements. An
ALJ has broad discretion over the conduct of hearings, including the timing and
admission of evidence. Notably, under §8-43-207(1)(i) C.R.S., an ALJ may grant
reasonable extensions of time for the taking of any action contained in the article for
good cause shown. Factors including timeliness, diligence, prejudice to opposing

parties, and the probative value of the additional evidence are significant when
determining whether good cause exists.
The critical inquiry in the present matter is whether Claimant’s work activities on
July 19, 2025 caused a right shoulder injury. The condition of Claimant’s right shoulder
is not the pivotal inquiry in determining compensability. Additional diagnostic testing will
not provide material or probative information regarding the cause of Claimant’s right
shoulder condition. Moreover, Claimant has not explained why the MRI testing could not
have been reasonably performed or the results obtained prior to the May 17, 2026
hearing in this matter. Finally, Respondents did not have an opportunity to address the
MRI findings on the date of the hearing. Accordingly, Claimant’s request to reopen the
evidentiary record and extend the due date for filing position statements is denied. The
evidence is closed and position statements were due by May 28, 2026.
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant is a 40-year-old Massage Therapist who alleges an injury to her
right shoulder while performing a couple’s massage on July 19, 2025. She detailed that
she went to work on July 19, 2025 and her last client of the day was a two-hour couple’s
massage. Claimant conducted a deep tissue massage on the male. She finished the
massage and performed closing duties, including folding laundry and preparing the
massage room for the next day.
2. Claimant went home, rested, showered and prepared for bed. She laid
down in bed on her right side. Claimant lifted her arm above her head and across her
body. She noticed a sharp pain in the anterior aspect of her right shoulder. Claimant
attributed her pain to simply overworking after seven or eight hours of full-scheduled
hands-on massages.
3. Claimant went to work on the following day of July 20, 2025. She
performed a deep tissue massage and completed her shift. She did not notice any
additional pain after work on July 20, 2025.
4. Claimant’s last day working for Employer was July 20, 2026. Although she
was scheduled for two additional shifts, she called out from work due to illness.
Claimant had emailed Employer on either July 16 or 17, 2025 and informed them that

she was resigning as of July 26, 2025. She had accepted another position at Wellness
Spa RX as a massage therapist with a start date of August 1, 2025.
5. Claimant acknowledged she did not report her injury to Employer’s
General Manager Sabrina Salazar or the lead therapist on either July 19, 2025 or July
20, 2025 because she did not realize she had an issue to report.
6. Claimant worked at two other massage facilities before she started
developing pain in her right shoulder in October 2025. She did not seek treatment for
her right shoulder until November 19, 2025.
7. On November 20, 2025 Claimant reported her right shoulder injury to Ms.
Salazar. Ms. Salazar noted that at no time did the other masseuse, , who
was in the couple’s massage with Claimant on the alleged date of injury, report that
Claimant suffered an injury.
8. On April 15, 2026 Claimant underwent an Independent Medical
Examination (IME) with Douglas C. Scott, M.D. Dr. Scott prepared a report and testified
at the hearing in this matter. He considered Claimant’s medical history and mechanism
of injury. Claimant told Dr. Scott that during the July 19, 2025 massage she did not feel
pain, popping or experience a specific injury to her right shoulder. Claimant detailed that
she did not feel symptoms during any of the massages on July 19, 2025. There was no
specific injurious event.
9. Claimant acknowledged the first time she felt pain was when she was at
home, lying in bed, moving her arm across her body. She specifically experienced a
sharp pain on the front side of her right shoulder. Claimant was able to complete the
deep tissue massage the following day with no pain or popping in her shoulder. She
recounted that during her work with a subsequent Employer, Wellness Spa Rx, she
started to gradually feel soreness in the anterior right shoulder without a specific injury
or event.
10. Dr. Scott noted that on January 21, 2026 Claimant underwent an MRI of
the right upper extremity. He explained that the imaging revealed findings of partial
subscapularis tearing, tendinosis, bursitis and AC joint osteoarthritis. Dr. Scott remarked
the diagnosis was unrelated to the alleged work injury. He commented that the
radiologist’s reading of the MRI scan “suggests that the findings of partial subscapularis

tearing, tendinosis, bursitis and AC joint osteoarthritis were chronic and possibly all of
these findings pre-existed 7/19/2025.” Dr. Scott also explained that, if Claimant suffered
a rotator cuff tear on July 19, 2025, she would not have been able to perform massages
the following day without reported pain or dysfunction.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
1. The purpose of the “Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado” (Act) is to
assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical benefits to injured
workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of any litigation. §8-
40-102(1), C.R.S. A claimant in a Workers' Compensation claim has the burden of
proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. §8-42-101, C.R.S.
A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering
all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 197
Colo. 306, 592 P.2d 792 (1979); People v. M.A., 104 P.3d 273, 275 (Colo. App. 2004).
The facts in a Workers' Compensation case are not interpreted liberally in favor of either
the rights of the injured worker or the rights of the employer. §8-43-201, C.R.S. A
Workers' Compensation case is decided on its merits. §8-43-201, C.R.S.
2. The Judge’s factual findings concern only evidence that is dispositive of
the issues involved; the Judge has not addressed every piece of evidence that might
lead to a conflicting conclusion and has rejected evidence contrary to the above findings
as unpersuasive. See Magnetic Engineering, Inc. v. ICAO, 5 P.3d 385, 389 (Colo. App.
2000).
3. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness’ testimony and actions; the
reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the testimony and
actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has been contradicted; and
bias, prejudice, or interest. See Prudential Insurance Co. v. Cline, 98 Colo. 275, 57 P.2d
1205 (1936); CJI, Civil 3:16 (2007).
4. For a claim to be compensable under the Act, a claimant has the burden of
proving that he suffered a disability that was proximately caused by an injury arising out
of and within the course and scope of employment. §8-41-301(1)(c) C.R.S.; In re

Swanson, W.C. No. 4-589-645 (ICAO, Sept. 13, 2006). Proof of causation is a threshold
requirement that an injured employee must establish by a preponderance of the evidence
before any compensation is awarded. Faulkner v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 12 P.3d 844,
846 (Colo. App. 2000); Singleton v. Kenya Corp., 961 P.2d 571, 574 (Colo. App. 1998).
The question of causation is generally one of fact for determination by the Judge.
Faulkner, 12 P.3d at 846.
5. A pre-existing condition or susceptibility to injury does not disqualify a claim
if the employment aggravates, accelerates or combines with the pre-existing condition to
produce a need for medical treatment. Duncan v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 107 P.3d
999, 1001 (Colo. App. 2004). A compensable injury is one that causes disability or the
need for medical treatment. City of Boulder v. Payne, 162 Colo. 345, 426 P.2d 194 (1967);
Mailand v. PSC Indus. Outsourcing LP, W.C. No. 4-898-391-01, (ICAO, Aug. 25, 2014).
6. Section 8-41-301(1)(c), C.R.S. requires that an injury be “proximately
caused by an injury or occupational disease arising out of and in the course of the
employee’s employment.” Thus, the claimant is required to prove a direct causal
relationship between the injury and the disability and need for treatment. However, the
industrial injury need not be the sole cause of the disability if the injury is a significant,
direct, and consequential factor in the disability. See Subsequent Injury Fund v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 131 P.3d 1224 (Colo. App. 2006); Joslins Dry Goods Co. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 21 P.3d 866 (Colo. App. 2001).
7. The mere fact a claimant experiences symptoms while performing work
does not require the inference that there has been an aggravation or acceleration of a
pre-existing condition. See Cotts v. Exempla, Inc., W.C. No. 4-606-563 (ICAO, Aug. 18,
2005). Rather, the symptoms could represent the “logical and recurrent consequence” of
the pre-existing condition. See F.R. Orr Construction v. Rinta, 717 P.2d 965 (Colo. App.
1985); Chasteen v. King Soopers, Inc., W.C. No. 4-445-608 (ICAO, Apr. 10, 2008). As
explained in Scully v. Hooters of Colorado Springs, W.C. No. 4-745-712 (ICAO, Oct. 27,
2008), simply because a claimant’s symptoms arise after the performance of a job
function does not necessarily create a causal relationship based on temporal proximity.
The panel in Scully noted that “correlation is not causation,” and merely because a

coincidental correlation exists between the claimant’s work and symptoms does not mean
there is a causal connection between the claimant’s injury and work activities.
8. The provision of medical care based on a claimant’s report of symptoms
does not establish an injury but only demonstrates that the claimant claimed an injury.
Washburn v. City Market, W.C. No. 5-109-470 (ICAO, June 3, 2020). Moreover, a referral
for medical care may be made so that the respondent would not forfeit its right to select
the medical providers if the claim is later deemed compensable. Id. Although a physician
may provide diagnostic testing, treatment, and work restrictions based on a claimant’s
reported symptoms, there is no mandate that the claimant suffered a compensable injury.
Fay v. East Penn Manufacturing Co., Inc., W.C. No. 5-108-430-001 (ICAO, Apr. 24,
2020); see Snyder v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 942 P.2d 1337, 1339 (Colo. App. 1997)
(“right to workers' compensation benefits, including medical payments, arises only when
an injured employee initially establishes, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the
need for medical treatment was proximately caused by an injury arising out of and in the
course of the employment”). While scientific evidence is not dispositive of compensability,
the ALJ may consider and rely on medical opinions regarding the lack of a scientific theory
supporting compensability. Savio House v. Dennis, 665 P.2d 141 (Colo. App. 1983);
Washburn v. City Market, W.C. No. 5-109-470 (ICAO, June 3, 2020).
9. Claimant has failed to establish by a preponderance of the evidence that
she suffered a compensable right shoulder injury during the course and scope of her
employment with Employer on July 19, 2025. Claimant acknowledged she did not feel
pain or symptoms while performing the deep tissue massage on the date of injury.
However, she mentioned a sharp pain at home when she moved her arm above her head
and across her body while lying in bed. Furthermore, Claimant acknowledged she felt no
pain the following day while completing her work duties with Employer including a deep
tissue massage. Notably, she did not feel symptoms in her right shoulder until October
2025 and did not seek treatment until November 19, 2025.
10. Dr. Scott commented that on January 21, 2026 Claimant underwent an MRI
of the right upper extremity. He persuasively explained that the imaging revealed findings
of partial subscapularis tearing, tendinosis, bursitis and AC joint osteoarthritis. Dr. Scott
remarked the diagnosis was unrelated to the alleged work injury. He commented that the

radiologist’s reading of the MRI scan “suggests that the findings of partial subscapularis
tearing, tendinosis, bursitis and AC joint osteoarthritis were chronic and possibly all of
these findings pre-existed 7/19/2025.” Furthermore, if Claimant suffered a rotator cuff tear
on July 19, 2025, she would not have been able to perform massages the following day
without reported pain or dysfunction.
11. Despite Claimant’s contention that her work activities caused her right
shoulder injury, the weight of the persuasive medical evidence reflects that she has failed
to demonstrate a causal connection to her employment. Initially, Claimant acknowledged
she felt no pain on July 20, 2025 while completing her work duties with Employer including
a deep tissue massage. Notably, although a temporal delay in the development of
symptoms and reporting is not dispositive of compensability, Claimant did not experience
significant right shoulder symptoms until October 2025 and did not seek treatment until
November 19, 2025. Finally, the January 21, 2026 right upper extremity MRI revealed
chronic findings. The preceding factors suggest that it is speculative to attribute her right
shoulder symptoms to her July 19, 2025 work activities. Accordingly, Claimant’s request
for Workers’ Compensation benefits is denied and dismissed.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant’s request for Workers’ Compensation benefits is denied and
dismissed.
2. Any issues not resolved in this Order are reserved for future
determination.
If you are dissatisfied with the Judge's order, you may file a Petition to Review
the order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the Judge's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it
within twenty (20) days after mailing or service of the order of the Judge; and (2) That
you mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. For

statutory reference, see section 8-43-301(2), C.R.S. For further information regarding
procedures to follow when filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may
access a petition to review form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.
