title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-313-561-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-313-561-001
Issues
Whether Respondent has established by a preponderance of the evidence
⮚
that Claimant was an independent contractor at the time of his July 28, 2025 work
injury?
The parties stipulated prior to hearing that if Claimant is determined to be
⮚
an Employee at the time of the injury, the claim is compensable.
The parties further stipulated that if the case is compensable, Claimant’s
⮚
medical treatment as documented in Exhibits 1-9 is reasonable medical treatment
necessary to cure and relieve the Claimant from the effects of the injury and
Respondents did not provide Claimant with a Designated Provider List after Claimant’s
injury.
The parties further stipulated that if the case is compensable, Claimant is
⮚
entitled to Temporary Total Disability (“TTD”) benefits beginning July 28, 2025 and the
average weekly wage (“AWW”) for Claimant is $443.77.
Findings of Fact
1. Uprooted Tree Care, LLC provides tree care and trimming services to
customers in the Cortez, Colorado area. Uprooted Tree Care, LLC (“Uprooted”) is
owned by Robert Schmidt. Mr. Schmidt testified at hearing that he hands out his
business card to potential clients in the Cortez area in an attempt to get the word out
about his services and then contracts with customers who contact him to perform tree
service work. Mr. Schmidt testified that he operates Uprooted out of his house.
1

2. Mr. Schmidt testified at hearing that his work for Uprooted included
arborist services, tree trimming and removal and general landscaping projects.
3. Mr. Schmidt testified that to assist him with his work, he would contract
with individuals who held themselves out to be arborist professionals to assist him on
his projects. One of the people Mr. Schmidt contracted with was .
testified at hearing that he was a “self contractor” for Uprooted.
testified that Uprooted was his primary source of income, but did do some automobile
detailing on weekends. testified he was originally a “groundsman” where his
job duties included loading the truck and clearing branches from the ground.
then became a rope assistant where his job duties included getting branches
and logs down safely. testified that he signed an agreement with Mr.
Schmidt after Claimant’s accident on July 28, 2025 identifying himself as an
independent contractor.
4. testified that in performing work for Uprooted, he would wear
a shirt with the Uprooted Tree Service, LLC name on it and would use equipment
provided by Mr. Schmidt. testified that normally when Uprooted would get a
job, Mr. Schmidt would drive the company truck to the job and the other workers would
ride in the truck with Mr. Schmidt. testified he was paid an hourly wage for
his work and the check was made out to individually. testified
that Mr. Schmidt would direct which people to perform which jobs on the job site.
5. Another person who worked for Uprooted was .
testified that he is an arborist working on everything that has to deal with
plant work or tree work. testified that he acquired the skills to be an
arborist over years of training and bookwork, and that his specialty within the arborist
trade is “dead work” over power lines. runs his own business named
Andreason Custom Contracting. He testified that Mr. Schmidt would contact
when he needed assistance in dead work over power lines, and that it was
clear that was an independent contractor contracted to perform work on
specific jobs within his specialty. usually charged by the job, but
2

sometimes worked by the hour for jobs contracted with Uprooted. had
all of his own tools and gear, though Respondent sometimes supplied chain saws or
other gear to , if the tools and equipment had on the job
site were not suitable for the particular job for which he was contracted.
testified that Respondent sometimes paid by check and sometimes paid by cash, and
that payments via check were made to personally.
6. testified that he used his own independent judgment as to
how to perform the jobs for which he was contracted, Respondent did not instruct him
as to how to perform the duties required, and that he was not under the control or
direction of Respondent. testified that he received an IRS 1099-NEC at
the end of every year for which he performed services for Respondent.
7. Mr. Schmidt testified at hearing that he hired to come work for
Uprooted when Claimant was living in Missouri. Mr. Schmidt testified he offered
Claimant temporary housing in his own home where he provided a room in his house by
having his children share a room. Mr. Schmidt testified he would offer Claimant work,
which was generally accepted by Claimant. Mr. Schmidt provided Claimant with
transportation to the job site. Mr. Schmidt noted in his testimony that Claimant had
some personal safety equipment and personal tools for doing the arborist work. Mr.
Schmidt testified that if here was heavier duty equipment or larger chainsaws that were
needed for a project, that equipment would be provided by Uprooted.
8. Mr. Schmidt testified at hearing that if Claimant was performing the
landscaping jobs, Claimant would need to use lawn mowers, wheel barrows, weed
trimmers and shovels provided by Uprooted. Mr. Schmidt testified that did
not have a motor vehicle to get any equipment to a job site.
9. Mr. Schmidt testified the pay rate was based on daily work rate, but later
admitted that in interrogatories he reported that workers were provided a $25 per hour
rate, which equated to $200 per day for an eight (8) hour day.
10. Mr. Schmidt testified that he would set a quality standard for the work
done and definitely set a safety standard and protocols for those working for Uprooted.
3

11. Mr. Schmidt discussed general conversations about why Uprooted could
not afford to have full-time or part time employees. Mr. Schmidt testified he spoke to
Claimant about how Claimant was an independent contractor for Uprooted. Mr. Schmidt
testified at hearing that he instructed each worker at to what duties each person did on
the job and would point out the scope of each job along with confirming completion of
the scope of each job before a job was complete and the worker was to be paid.
12. Mr. Schmidt testified he did not require Claimant to work exclusively for
Uprooted. Records entered into evidence at hearing show that after Claimant moved to
Colorado, he worked for Uprooted for 31 hours in February 2025, 32 hours in March
2025, 61 hours in April 2025, 49 hours in May 2025 and 103 hours in June 2025. The
records show that Claimant had worked for Uprooted for 76 hours in July 2025 prior to
his injury. Claimant testified he did not perform other work for compensation, but did
construct a chicken coop for his girlfriend at some point.
13. Mr. Schmidt testified that on the day of the injury he left his climbing gear
at his home and that Claimant was hired as a ground man on the day of the injury. Mr.
Schmidt testified when he came back to the job site he saw Claimant in the tree cutting
branches. Mr. Schmidt was in the process of securing the area when he saw the
accident occur.
14. Mr. Schmidt testified he would provide people working on the project with
Uprooted Tree Care shirts that would be worn when person was working for Uprooted.
Mr. Schmidt further testified that , who had his own company, would not
wear the Uprooted shirt but would wear company shirt.
15. Mr. Schmidt testified at hearing that Uprooted did not have Workers’
Compensation insurance. Claimant did not have a signed contract with Uprooted as
contemplated by Section 8-40-202(2)(b)(I) and (III), C.R.S.
16. Claimant testified at hearing that he was hired by Mr. Schmidt after they
had connected through some rock climbing friends. Claimant testified he was at that
point working in Missouri performing tree trimming for a company in Missouri and was
4

looking to try to move back to Colorado. Claimant had sent Mr. Schmidt videos of the
tree trimming work he was performing in Missouri.
17. Claimant was injured on July 28, 2025 when he was trimming a tree that
was contracted by Uprooted and a branch broke causing Claimant to fall 40 feet before
landing on the ground. Claimant was taken by ambulance to Mercy Medical Center
before being airlifted to St. Mary’s Hospital in Grand Junction, Colorado.
18. Respondent argues at hearing that Claimant was an independent
contractor for Uprooted arguing the Respondent did not provide tools or benefits to
Claimant, Respondent did not dictate the time of performance of Claimant’s duties and
had the option of denying the work being offered to him if he chose not to perform the
work. The ALJ is not persuaded.
19. The facts in this case establish that while Claimant had some of his own
tools to perform the work provided by Uprooted, many of the tools, including, but not
limited to, lawn mowers, shovels, wheel barrows and larger chain saws were provided
by Uprooted. The evidence establishes that Claimant was paid hourly for his work and
was paid directly to Claimant as opposed to a company name. While Respondent
argues that they did not dictate the schedule and time for the performance of the work,
Claimant was transported to the job by Mr. Schmidt in a company truck, which suffices
to establish that Uprooted was dictating the time of performance by driving Claimant to
and from the job site. The ALJ further finds that Mr. Schmidt controlled the work
Claimant was assigned by determining which project Claimant would perform and
whether that included tree trimming, landscaping or lawn maintenance. Additionally, for
any lawn maintenance job assigned to Claimant, Claimant would be required to use the
mowers and other tools provided by Uprooted. Moreover, while on the job site,
Claimant was provided with a shirt that advertised Uprooted services.
20. Based on the totality of the evidence presented at hearing, the ALJ finds
that Respondents have failed to overcome the presumption of employment and have
failed establish that Claimant was performing work as an independent contractor at the
time of his injury.
5

Conclusions of Law
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101,
et seq., C.R.S. is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of
litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden of proving
entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-43-201, C.R.S. A
preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering all
of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 592
P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’ compensation case must be interpreted
neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of
respondents; and a workers’ compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-
201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law judge.
University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637 (Colo. App.
2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a contrary inference, it
is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make credibility determinations, and
draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at 641. When determining credibility,
the fact finder should consider, among other things, the consistency or inconsistency of
the witness's testimony and actions; the reasonableness or unreasonableness
(probability or improbability) of the testimony and actions; the motives of the witness;
whether the testimony has been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential
Ins. Co. v. Cline, 57 P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals
Office, 183 P.3d 684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert
testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim Appeals
Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is subject to
conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting part or none of
the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n, 441 P.2d 21 (Colo.
1968).
6

C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to
be dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has rejected
evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
D. Any individual who performs services for pay for another shall be deemed
to be an employee, irrespective of whether the common-law relationship of master and
servant exists, unless such individual is free from control and direction in the
performance of the service, both under the contract for performance of service and in
fact and such individual is customarily engaged in an independent trade, occupation,
profession, or business related to the service performed. § 8-40-202(2)(a).
E. If the evidence establishes that Claimant was performing services for pay,
and there is no written document establishing Claimant’s independent contractor status,
the burden of proof rests upon the Respondent to rebut the presumption that Claimant
was an employee. Baker v. BV Properties, LLC, W.C. No. 4-618-214 (Aug. 25, 2006).
The question of whether Respondents have overcome the presumption and established
that Claimant was an independent contractor is one of fact for the ALJ. Nelson v.
Industrial Claim Appeals Off. of Colo., 981 P.2d 210 (Colo.App.1998).
F. Section 8-40-202(2)(b)(II), C.R.S., enumerates nine factors to be
considered in evaluating whether an individual is deemed an employee or independent
contractor. Under that section, to demonstrate independent contractor status and to
prove independence from direction and control in the performance the job by the worker
it must be shown that the person for whom services are performed does not: (A) require
the individual to work exclusively for a single person or company, (B) does not establish
a quality standard for the individual’s work, (C) does not pay a salary or hourly rate
instead of a fixed contract rate, (D) is not able to terminate the individual’s employment
without liability during the contract period, (E) provides no more than minimal training to
the individual, (F) does not provide tools or benefits, other than materials; (G) does not
dictate the time of performance other than a completion schedule and a range of
7

agreeable work hours, (H) does not pay individually rather than under a trade or
business name, and (I) does not combine its business with the business of the
individual. § 8-40-202(2)(b)(2). However, the existence of any one of these factors is not
conclusive evidence that the individual is an employee. § 8-40-202(2)(b)(III). Thus, it is
not necessary to satisfy all nine criteria in order to demonstrate that an individual is an
independent contractor and not an employee. Nelson v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office,
981 P.2d 210, 212 (Colo. App. 1998).
G. As found, the evidence establishes that Claimant was under the direction
and control of Employer in performing the duties of a tree trimmer and landscaper. As
found, Employer provided Claimant many of the tools to perform his work, including
lawn mowers, shovels, wheel barrows and larger chain saws were. As found, the
evidence establishes that Claimant was paid hourly for his work and was paid directly to
Claimant as opposed to a company name. As found, Respondent dictated the schedule
and time for the performance of the work, by transporting Claimant to the job by Mr.
Schmidt in a company truck. Moreover, while on the job site, Claimant was provided
with a shirt that advertised Uprooted services while Claimant was working.
H. As found, Mr. Schmidt would assign the various jobs to Claimant to
perform and would determine if the job involved landscaping, lawn maintenance or tree
services. As found, Mr. Schmidt paid Claimant an hourly rate for his work and made the
checks out personally to Claimant.
I. As found, based on the totality of the evidence, the ALJ determines that
Respondent has failed to overcome the presumption that the Claimant is an employee
by a preponderance of the evidence and was engaged in an independent trade for
Respondent.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant is an employee of Employer.
8

2. Respondent shall pay for the reasonable medical treatment necessary to
cure and relieve Claimant from the effects of his injury on July 28, 2025.
3. Respondent shall pay Claimant TTD benefits based on an AWW of
$443.47 commencing July 28, 2025 and continuing until terminated by law or statute.
4. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.

title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-329-923-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-329-923-001
Issues
1. Whether Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence
that he suffered a compensable left knee injury on February 3, 2026 during the course
and scope of employment with Employer.
2. Whether Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that he
is entitled to receive reasonable and necessary medical benefits that are causally
related to his February 3, 2026 left knee injury.
Findings of Fact
1. On February 3, 2026 Claimant worked for the Colorado State University
(CSU) Police Department as a Campus Security Officer (CSO). He explained that CSOs
are security personnel who call dispatch to report unusual or suspicious activities on
campus.
2. On February 3, 2026 Claimant was working a “safe walk” shift. His job duties
on a safe walk shift involved being on-call for any student who requested an escort while
walking around campus or to/from their car or apartment within a three-block radius of
campus. The CSO’s acted as a visible deterrent on campus and radioed any suspicious
activity to the campus police department. Claimant explained that, if there were no
students to escort, the CSO’s patrolled or “free roamed” campus for suspicious activity.
3. After doing some homework, Claimant and coworker
decided to explore campus. Notably, around 10:00 pm, Claimant and
accessed the rooftop of the Warner building. To reach the rooftop of the Warner building,
they proceeded through a locked door with a sign that read, “Authorized personnel only.”
Claimant testified that he was following because she had previously been up
to the roof. Nevertheless, he acknowledged that he “definitely” should not be up on the
roof.
4. Claimant and proceeded up the restricted staircase and through
a hatch door. They ultimately reached the roof of the Warner building. Once on the third-

floor roof, they climbed a ladder to the fourth-floor roof and took some photographs.
Claimant remarked that going on roofs appeared common among more senior CSOs.
Notably, co-workers sent photos from atop the Warner building in a CSO group chat.
5. Claimant and eventually made their way off the roof. They
climbed down the ladder and decided to take a more direct route back to the hatch door.
The route involved dropping down off a small ledge.
6. After climbing off the ledge, Claimant lost his footing and slipped on ice. He
heard his knee pop and crumbled to the ground. Claimant was subsequently diagnosed
with a left knee dislocation.
7. Because Claimant was unable to move, called two Field Training
Officers (FTOs) who were more experienced CSOs. CTOs and met them
on the third-floor rooftop and helped them decide what to do next. Claimant was ultimately
rescued and hoisted off the roof by a team of firefighters, police officers, and EMTs.
8. Claimant was taken by ambulance to the emergency department at Banner
Health. He was diagnosed with a patellar fracture. Claimant ultimately underwent surgery
to repair his left knee.
9. Claimant did not have permission to access the rooftop of the Warner
building. He understood that he was not considered authorized personnel for purposes of
rooftop access. Specifically, when asked if there were areas on campus he was told not
to access, Claimant responded,
A: I can’t think of all of them at the top of my head, but definitely roofs. I’m
guessing like any other restricted areas that had visual signs I probably
wasn’t supposed to go.
TR. p. 10:20-22.
Furthermore, Claimant testified,
Q: But you, you knew you shouldn’t be on the roof though. Correct?
A: Oh yeah, definitely.
TR. p. 18:9-11.

10. The key that unlocked the door providing rooftop access to the Warner
building also unlocked various other doors around campus, some of which Claimant was
permitted to access as part of his job. Although Claimant had a key that granted him
rooftop access, he lacked authorization to access rooftops.
11. Sergeant Ramsey Crochet of the CSU Police Department testified at the
hearing in this matter. He explained that the primary function of the safewalk shift was
walking students home when requested. The secondary function was to observe and
report suspicious campus activity. Sergeant Crochet confirmed that the CSOs on a
safewalk shift would observe by walking around campus and report by radioing any
suspicious activity into dispatch. The CSU Training Guide used by security officers states:
“When you do not have a safewalk, you will patrol campus. While patrolling, call out
anything suspicious, and check buildings (at least the doors, if it is open, you can also go
check the inside).”
12. Sergeant Crochet remarked that the training manual specified the
procedure for addressing unsecured roof access. He commented that the Training Guide
prohibits rooftop access. Sergeant Crochet maintained that CSO’s are directed to contact
the dispatch center when they encounter unsecured rooftop access. Officers are then
sent over to clear the roof. CSOs are not permitted to clear roofs based on the “unsecured
access” provision of the Training Guide on Respondents’ Exhibits page 56.
13. Sergeant Crochet emphasized that CSOs were not permitted to be on the
roofs of campus buildings. He testified to the following:
Q: So, just to clarify did [Claimant] have authorization to be on the roof?
A: No, sir.
Q: Was there any operational necessity for him being on the roof?
A: No, sir.
Q: Were you aware that any supervisors had given him approval to be on
the roof?
A: No, sir.

Q: Was this a circumvention of the security controls and contrary to policy
as detailed in the CSO training manual?
A: Yes, sir.
TR. p. 32:1-12.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
1. The purpose of the “Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado” (Act) is to
assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical benefits to injured
workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of any litigation. §8-
40-102(1), C.R.S. A claimant in a Workers' Compensation claim has the burden of
proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. §8-42-101, C.R.S.
A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering
all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 197
Colo. 306, 592 P.2d 792 (1979); People v. M.A., 104 P.3d 273, 275 (Colo. App. 2004).
The facts in a Workers' Compensation case are not interpreted liberally in favor of either
the rights of the injured worker or the rights of the employer. §8-43-201, C.R.S. A
Workers' Compensation case is decided on its merits. §8-43-201, C.R.S.
2. The Judge’s factual findings concern only evidence that is dispositive of
the issues involved; the Judge has not addressed every piece of evidence that might
lead to a conflicting conclusion and has rejected evidence contrary to the above findings
as unpersuasive. See Magnetic Engineering, Inc. v. ICAO, 5 P.3d 385, 389 (Colo. App.
2000).
3. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness’ testimony and actions; the
reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the testimony and
actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has been contradicted; and
bias, prejudice, or interest. See Prudential Insurance Co. v. Cline, 98 Colo. 275, 57 P.2d
1205 (1936); CJI, Civil 3:16 (2007).
4. For a claim to be compensable under the Act, a claimant has the burden of
proving that he suffered a disability that was proximately caused by an injury arising out
of and within the course and scope of employment. §8-41-301(1)(c) C.R.S.; In re

Swanson, WC 4-589-645 (ICAO, Sept. 13, 2006). Proof of causation is a threshold
requirement that an injured employee must establish by a preponderance of the evidence
before any compensation is awarded. Faulkner v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 12 P.3d 844,
846 (Colo. App. 2000); Singleton v. Kenya Corp., 961 P.2d 571, 574 (Colo. App. 1998).
The question of causation is generally one of fact for determination by the Judge.
Faulkner, 12 P.3d at 846.
5. A pre-existing condition or susceptibility to injury does not disqualify a claim
if the employment aggravates, accelerates or combines with the pre-existing condition to
produce a need for medical treatment. Duncan v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 107 P.3d
999, 1001 (Colo. App. 2004). A compensable injury is one that causes disability or the
need for medical treatment. City of Boulder v. Payne, 162 Colo. 345, 426 P.2d 194 (1967);
Mailand v. PSC Indus. Outsourcing LP, WC 4-898-391-01, (ICAO, Aug. 25, 2014).
6. When the employer asserts a personal deviation from employment “the
issue is whether the activity giving rise to the injury constituted a deviation from
employment so substantial as to remove it from the employment relationship.” Roache v.
Indus. Comm’n, 729 P.2d 991 (Colo. App. 1986); In Re Laroc, WC 4-783-889 (ICAO, Feb.
1, 2010). If an employee substantially deviates from the mandatory or incidental duties of
employment so that he is acting for his sole benefit at the time of injury, his claim is not
compensable. Kater v. Indus. Comm’n, 729 P.2d 746 (Colo. App. 1986). The issue is thus
whether the “claimant’s conduct constitutes such a deviation from the circumstances and
conditions of the employment that the claimant stepped aside from his job and was
performing an activity for his sole benefit.” In Re Laroc, WC 4-783-889 (ICAO, Feb. 1,
2010); see Panera Bread, LLC v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 141 P.3d 970 (Colo. App.
2006). It is thus not essential that the activities of an employee emanate from an obligatory
job function or result in a specific benefit to the employer for a claim to be compensable.
City of Boulder v. Streeb, 706 P.2d 786 (Colo. 1985). When the employee’s personal
errand is concluded, the deviation ends, and the employee is once again covered by
Workers’ Compensation. Skywest Airlines, Inc. v. indus. Claim Appeals Off., 487 P.3d
1267, 1272 (Colo. App. 2020).
7. Where the alleged deviation from employment involves “horseplay,” our
courts apply a four-part test to determine whether the resulting injury is compensable. In

Lori’s Family Dining v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 907 P.2d 715, 718 (Colo. App. 1995)
the Colorado Court of Appeals enumerated the following four factors:
(1) the extent and seriousness of the deviation; (2) the completeness of the
deviation, i.e., whether it was commingled with the performance of a duty or
involved an abandonment of duty; (3) the extent to which the practice of
horseplay had become an accepted part of the employment; and (4) the extent
to which the nature of the employment may be expected to include some
horseplay.
No single factor is determinative, and the claimant need not prove the existence of every
factor to establish compensability. Panera Bread, LLC v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 141
P.3d 970 (Colo. App. 2006); see Alvarez v. Rifle Tequilas, Inc., WC 5-050-687 (ICAO,
July 6, 2018).
8. In analyzing the first factor of the four-part test, the court evaluates whether
the deviation was prolonged or geographically distant from the place of employment.
Lori’s Family Dining, 907 P.2d at 718. Here, Claimant admitted that he and his coworker
accessed the roof, took pictures on the third-floor rooftop, then proceeded to the fourth-
floor rooftop for more photographs. They then hung “out up there for about 10-15 minutes”
before deciding to make their way back down. Claimant’s rooftop visit was not
straightforward but an intricate route consisting of accessing an elevator and multiple
floors of the building, proceeding up a restricted stairwell, and navigating a hatch door.
The amount of time Claimant spent accessing and hanging out on the roof constitutes a
prolonged deviation.
9. Although the building was geographically situated within the boundaries of
his employment, being on the rooftop of the building is geographically distant from where
he was expected to be performing his duties. His primary duty on a safewalk shift was to
provide a safe escort for people and act as a visible deterrent on campus. His presence
on the ground was thus necessary to successfully perform his job duties. Instead,,
Claimant accessed a fourth-floor rooftop by proceeding through a locked door clearly
marked "Authorized personnel only" and climbing a ladder. Although Claimant’s role
involved "free-roaming" patrol, the act of bypassing restricted access to reach a frozen
rooftop to take photographs late at night is a serious departure from the primary duty of

acting as a visible deterrent on campus. Therefore, this element of the four-part test
weighs in favor of Respondents’ contention that Claimant substantially deviated from his
job responsibilities, such that he was no longer within the scope of his employment when
he was injured on February 3, 2026.
10. The second factor relates to whether the deviation was an abandonment of
duties. Lori’s Family Dining, Inc. 907 P.2d at 718. Claimant argued that, because he was
still able to see campus and his radio worked on the rooftop, he could still observe and
report suspicious activities on campus. However, Claimant’s main objective in accessing
the roof was to take photos, not to observe suspicious activity. Respondents argued, and
Sergeant Crochet and Claimant confirmed, that Claimant’s main responsibilities on a
safewalk shift were to serve as an escort to students and act as a visible deterrent on
campus. Specifically, when asked what patrolling campus entailed, Claimant stated,
A: You’re pretty much able to free roam campus. That’s the whole point of
safe walk is to be providing, I’m trying to think of the word, not authority,
but like a presence around campus at night.
TR. p. 9:20-23.
11. Claimant also agreed that one of the main goals of his job “was to increase
response time for on-duty officers.” Claimant’s safewalk shift required him to be available
for student escorts. However, while up on a rooftop Claimant could not patrol campus for
suspicious activity, act as a visible deterrent on campus, and increase response time for
on-duty officers. Claimant had effectively abandoned his duties to take photos while on
top of the roof. Being on a fourth-floor roof made Claimant less available for calls and
invisible to the campus community he was tasked to protect. Dropping off a ledge for a
"more direct route" back to the hatch was a personal choice for convenience or recreation,
not a fulfillment of employment duties. Sergeant Crochet emphasized that an officer on a
fourth-floor roof is not visible to someone on the ground and is "delayed" in responding to
calls, effectively nullifying his primary duty. Therefore, this element of the four-part test
weighs in favor of Respondents’ contention that Claimant substantially deviated from his
job responsibilities such that he was no longer within the scope of his employment.

12. The third factor evaluates whether Claimant’s conduct had become an
accepted part of the employment. The court of appeals in Lori’s Family Dining, Inc.
reasoned that horseplay was “customary and countenanced by the employer.” Lori’s
Family Dining, Inc. 907 P.2d at 718. Here, despite Claimant’s testimony that other CSOs
had sent rooftop photos within a chat, he was not “comfortable” accessing rooftops even
though others had been doing it. Furthermore, Sergeant Crochet testified that no one at
a leadership level was aware that officers were accessing rooftops for photography. The
lack of management's acquiescence to this behavior weighs against finding it an
"accepted part" of the workplace. Therefore, this element of the four-part test weighs in
favor of Respondents’ contention that Claimant substantially deviated from his job
responsibilities, such that he was no longer within the scope of his employment on the
night of his left knee injury.
13. The final factor is the extent to which the nature of the employment may be
expected to include some horseplay. Lori’s Family Dining, Inc. 907 P.2d at 718. Here,
CSOs are college students who receive keys to areas of campus that they otherwise
would be unable to access. There may be some horseplay amongst the group such as
running out on the field at the football stadium like Claimant had done earlier in the night
on February 3, 2026. Based on their ability to explore and “free-roam,” it is reasonable to
assume that the CSOs may participate in horseplay in the form of activities that are not
strictly prohibited. However, as Sergeant Crochet explained, roof access is strictly
prohibited, and Claimant was not considered “authorized personnel.” Climbing up to a
roof thus falls outside the scope of any horseplay Employer should reasonably expect
from the CSOs. Further, it is clear from Sergeant Crochet’s testimony that he did not learn
that the CSOs had been accessing rooftops until after this incident, and he expected his
CSOs to utilize better judgment. Therefore, this element of the four-part test weighs in
favor of Respondents’ contention that Claimant had substantially deviated from his job
responsibilities, such that he was no longer within the scope of employment.
14. The facts of the case in Orist, v. G4S Secure Solutions, WC 4-886-126-01
(ICAO, Aug. 17, 2012) closely mirror the facts in the present case. In Orist the claimant
was a custom protection officer (CPO) at a hospital. His training included an emphasis on
safety, and the training manual specifically warned against the dangers of horseplay.

During one of his shifts while patrolling, he climbed down from an open window-like space
on the third floor of the parking garage onto the third-floor roof. Claimant then jumped
from the third-floor roof to the second-floor roof and sustained a tibial fracture of the left
knee. At the hearing, the facility manager testified that there were limited times when it
would be necessary for a CPO to be on the roof such as when window washers or
repairmen needed access. The ALJ found that the claimant’s injuries arose out of and in
the course and scope of employment. However, the ICAO reversed because, although
part of the claimant’s job duties involved exploring the facility, his job did not include
jumping from one rooftop to another. Orist suggests that, while minor horseplay might be
expected in some security roles, rooftop jumping is not. Moreover, although there were
times when it was necessary for a CPO to access rooftops such as to let a repairman
onto the roof, those circumstances did not exist at the time he accessed the roof. The
ICAO concluded that the claimant’s act of jumping from rooftop to rooftop constituted a
substantial deviation, effectively removing him from the employment relationship. His
claim was thus denied as a matter of law.
15. Consistent with the holding in Orist, Claimant decided to access a restricted
rooftop. He subsequently dropped off a ledge that caused him to slip on ice and injure his
left knee. The nature of a campus security role does not reasonably encompass the risks
associated with navigating frozen rooftops for personal photography. Claimant’s
horseplay constituted a willful, significant deviation aimed solely at personal amusement
and was disconnected from work duties. His actions were a substantial deviation from the
mandatory and incidental functions of his employment. Because he was acting for his
sole benefit at the time of injury, the claim is not compensable. Accordingly, Claimant’s
claim for Workers’ Compensation benefits is denied and dismissed.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant’s request for Workers’ Compensation benefits is denied and
dismissed.
2. Any issues not resolved in this Order are reserved for future
determination.

If you are dissatisfied with the Judge's order, you may file a Petition to Review

mailing or service of the order, as indicated on certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the Judge's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it

title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-309-389-003
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-309-389-003
Issues
Whether Claimant proved by a preponderance of the evidence that he sustained
⮚
a compensable injury arising out of the course of his employment with Employer
on April 11, 2025.
Whether Claimant established by a preponderance of the evidence entitlement to
⮚
reasonable and necessary medical benefits to cure or relieve the effects of an
industrial injury.
If compensable, determination of Claimant’s authorized treating physician (ATP).
⮚
If compensable, whether Claimant established by a preponderance of the
⮚
evidence entitlement to temporary disability benefits.
If compensable, determination of Claimant’s average weekly wage (AWW).
⮚
Whether Claimant established that Respondent is subject to penalties for failure
⮚
to carry workers’ compensation insurance.
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant testified that on April 11, 2025, he was working for Employer removing
window trim when he heard a “snap” in his elbow. At approximately 9:00 a.m.,
Claimant sent a text message to Employer’s owner, Scott DeThomas indicating
that he had just injured his right shoulder and heard something snap while
removing window trim.
2. One of Claimant’s coworkers took him to the emergency department at UC
Health on April 11, 2025, where he was evaluated for acute shoulder pain that
occurred while he was removing siding. On examination, Claimant was noted to
have limited internal rotation of the right shoulder, with generalized tenderness.
The ER physician noted that Claimant’s presentation was most consistent with a
1

labrum tear or ligamentous injury, medical records also indicate Claimant may
have sustained a sprain. Claimant was discharged in a shoulder sling, with
instructions to rest and ice his shoulder, provided exercises for shoulder rotation,
and instructed to follow up with his primary care provider.
3. Between April 14, 2025 and April 18, 2025, Claimant and Mr. DeThomas
engaged in multiple text exchanges. On April 14, 2025, Claimant sent Mr.
DeThomas photos of the discharge instructions he received from UC Health. Mr.
DeThomas requested copies of work restrictions and indicated that his
“insurance does not cover unsubstantiated claims.” Claimant sent Mr. DeThomas
a note from UCHealth indicating that he may return to work on April 15, 2025.
4. In an April 15, 2025 text exchange, Claimant texted Mr. DeThomas: “I’ve never
been given any information on what doctors I can be seen by under workmen’s
comp.” To which Mr. DeThomas replied “…you haven’t asked and haven’t
provided any reason. Based on Fridays visit this wouldn’t have been a wc claim.
It said there might be a slight sprain and you’d be back to work today;” and
indicated “We can definitely make a claim if you believe it’s warranted. I’ve been
given no reason up to today when I asked you.”
5. Claimant then indicated that he needed a couple of days to recover and hopefully
return to working condition. Mr. DeThomas stated that “without a note or
diagnosis,” he could not pay Claimant and “a WC claim can’t proceed.” Mr.
DeThomas then requested that Claimant work at the office the following day
answering phones.
6. On April 17, 2025, Claimant was seen by Craig Lewis at County Line
Chiropractic, where he reported pain in his trapezius, right shoulder and arm,
chest and neck. It was noted that Claimant had limited right shoulder movement,
with difficulty hinging at the AC joint, and lifting from his deltoid. The treatment
Claimant received appears to have been directed to other body parts, including
his thoracic spine, lumbar spine, cervical spine, and hips.
7. On April 18, 2025, Claimant and Mr. DeThomas engaged in another text
exchange, Claimant again requested a list of physicians to see for a workers’
2

compensation claim. Claimant indicated he had contacted his primary care
provider and was informed that he did not treat worker’s compensation injuries.
Mr. DeThomas told Claimant to see his primary care physician as directed by the
ER physician, indicated that Claimant’s physician should speak to Employer’s
insurance agent, and sent Claimant the contact information for ,
who is apparently Employer’s insurance agent.
8. Claimant returned to County Line Chiropractic on April 30, 2025 with the same
complaints. Neither of the chiropractic records appear to document treatment
related to a ligamentous or labral injury to the right shoulder, with the exception
of applying a hot pack.
9. Respondent submitted a statement from in which
indicated that “A claim was not filed due to this being a nonwork-related injury
and was due to pre-existing condition or tissue degradation over time. Refusal to
return to work and was out of state on two separate occasions.” The remainder of
statement is a “timeline of events” which purports to set forth the
facts of what occurred regarding Claimant’s injury and claim. The vast majority of
statement appears to be information gathered from others, for
which his personal knowledge was not established, and what appears to be his
personal opinion that Claimant’s injury “could be due to a pre-existing condition.”
With the exception of explanation as to the rationale for not filing a
workers compensation claim, his statement is of no evidentiary value.
10. Mr. DeThomas testified that he believed Claimant had violated a safety rule by
climbing a ladder without a safety observer in violation of employer’s safety
policies, and that Claimant refused to return to work after his injury. However, no
credible evidence was admitted demonstrating that Claimant’s injury was caused
by or related to any alleged safety rule violation.
11. Claimant did not return to work for Employer following his injury. Claimant
submitted records indicating he returned to work from July 7, 2025 through the
present for Valiant Products Corporation. Claimant’s pay stub for the November
15 – 28, 2025 pay period shows Claimant’s year-to-date earnings of $20,766.98
3

at a regular rate of $26.00 per hour (i.e., 798.73 hours), the equivalent of
approximately twenty 40-hour work weeks. Claimant offered no credible evidence
demonstrating that he suffered a loss of earning capacity after July 7, 2025.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S., is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law
judge. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637
(Colo. App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a
contrary inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make
credibility determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at
641. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions;
the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has
been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Ins. Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert
testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim
4

Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is
subject to conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting
part or none of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n,
441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
Compensability
D. To establish a compensable injury an employee must prove by a preponderance
of the evidence that his injury arose out of the course and scope of employment
with his employer. § 8-41-301(1)(b), C.R.S. (2006); see City of Boulder v. Streeb,
706 P.2d 786, 791 (Colo. 1985). An injury occurs "in the course of” employment
when a claimant demonstrates that the injury occurred within the time and place
limits of his employment and during an activity that had some connection with his
work-related functions. Triad Painting Co. v. Blair, 812 P.2d 638, 641 (Colo.
1991). The "arising out of" requirement is narrower and requires the claimant to
demonstrate that the injury has its “origin in an employee's work-related functions
and is sufficiently related thereto to be considered part of the employee’s service
to the employer.” Popovich v. Irlando, 811 P.2d 379, 383 (Colo. 1991). A
compensable injury is one that causes disability or the need for medical
treatment. City of Boulder v. Payne, 426 P.2d 194 (1967); Mailand v. PSC Indus.
Outsourcing LP, W.C. No. 4-898-391-01, (ICAO Aug. 25, 2014).
E. Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence that he sustained
a work-related injury on April 11, 2025. Claimant credibly testified that he heard a
“pop” while removing window trim for Employer on April 11, 2025, and
experienced pain in his right shoulder. Claimant’s contemporaneous medical
records from UCHealth are consistent with the report, and demonstrate that
Claimant likely sustained, at a minimum, a shoulder sprain which required
5

treatment. Employer’s belief that Claimant sustained a “minor” sprain does not
render the injury non-compensable, nor excuse Employer from compliance with
the Workers’ Compensation Act.
F. Employer’s (or its insurance agent’s) apparent belief that Claimant’s shoulder
injury was the result of a pre-existing condition does not change the result. A pre-
existing disease or susceptibility to injury does not disqualify a claim if the
employment aggravates, accelerates, or combines with the pre-existing disease
to produce a disability or need for medical treatment. Duncan v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Office, 107 P.3d 999 (Colo. App. 2004); H & H Warehouse v. Vicory,
805 P.2d 1167 (Colo. App. 1990); Enriquez v. Americold, WC 4-960-513-01,
(ICAO, Oct. 2, 2015). “A compensable aggravation can be a worsened
preexisting condition, a trigger of symptoms from a dormant condition, an
acceleration of the natural course of the preexisting condition, or a combination
with the condition to produce disability.” Bryant v. Mesa Cty. Valley Sch. Dist. 51,
W.C. No. 5-102-109-001 (ICAO, Mar. 18, 2020).
G. “To prove an aggravation, a claimant need not show an injury objectively caused
any identifiable structural change to their underlying anatomy. Rather, a purely
symptomatic aggravation is a sufficient basis for an award of medical benefits if it
caused the claimant to need treatment he would not otherwise have required but
for the accident.” In re Claim of Frank O’Neil Cambria, W.C. No. 5-066-531-002
(ICAO May 7, 2019). Compensability of aggravation cases turns on whether work
activities made the preexisting condition worse in some manner or simply
demonstrated the natural progression of the preexisting condition. Bryant, supra.
H. Although the record contains no evidence that Claimant had a pre-existing
shoulder condition, even if Claimant’s injury was an aggravation of a pre-existing
condition, it constitutes a compensable injury under the Colorado Workers’
Compensation Act.
Medical Treatment
I. Under section 8-42-101(1)(a), C.R.S., employers are liable for authorized
medical treatment that is reasonable and necessary to cure or relieve the effects
6

of the industrial injury. See Owens v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 49 P.3d 1187,
1188 (Colo. App. 2002). Because Claimant has established that he sustained a
compensable injury, he is entitled to all reasonable, and necessary medical
treatment rendered to cure or relieve the effects of his industrial injury.
J. Employer is therefore liable for all of Claimant’s reasonable and necessary
medical expenses related to the April 11, 2025 injury, pursuant to the Colorado
Medical Fee Schedule.
Authorized Treating Physician
K. Section 8-43-404(5)(a), C.R.S., permits an employer or insurer to select the
treating physician in the first instance. Yeck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 996
P.2d 228 (Colo. App. 1999). However, the Colorado Workers’ Compensation Act
requires that respondents must provide injured workers with a list of at least four
designated treatment providers. §8-43-404(5)(a)(I)(A), C.R.S. Rule 8-2 (A)(2)
clarifies that, “[a] copy of the written designated provider list must be given to the
injured worker in a verifiable manner within seven (7) business days following the
date the employer has notice of the injury.” The term “business days” refers to
any day other than a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday. W.C.R.P. 1-2 (C).
L. An employer is deemed notified of an injury when it has “some knowledge of the
accompanying facts connecting the injury or illness with the employment and
indicating to a reasonably conscientious manager that the case might involve a
potential compensation claim.” Bunch v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 148 P.3d
381, 383 (Colo. App. 2006). If upon notice of the injury the employer does not
timely designate an ATP, the right of selection passes to the claimant. Rogers v.
Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 746 P.2d 565 (Colo. App. 1987), see also W.C.R.P.
8-2 (E) (“If the employer fails to supply the required designated provider list in
accordance with this rule, the injured worker may select an authorized treating
physician or chiropractor of their choosing.”) Where a claimant has signified “by
words or conduct that he has chosen a physician to treat the industrial injury,” he
has made physician “selection.” In re Claim of Murphy-Tafoya, W.C. No. 5-153-
600-001 (ICAO, Sept. 1, 2021).
7

M. The evidence establishes that Claimant informed Employer, through Mr.
DeThomas of his injury on April 11, 2025. Accordingly, Employer was obligated
to provide Claimant with a list of designated providers within seven business
days. Employer has neither presented evidence nor claimed that a list of medical
providers was delivered to Claimant. That Employer did not believe Claimant’s
injury was significant, or that Employer’s insurance agent believed Claimant had
aggravated a pre-existing condition does not relieve Employer of the obligation to
provide a designated provider list.
N. Claimant has established that Employer did not provide him a list of designated
providers as required by the Act. As such, the right of selection of designated
providers passed to Claimant.
O. The care Claimant received on April 11, 2025 constitutes emergency treatment
immediately following his injury for which Employer is liable. § 8-42-101(1)(a),
C.R.S.; Sims v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 797 P.2d 777 (Colo. App. 1990). The
evidence is unclear whether the treatment Claimant sought at County Line
Chiropractic was for his work-related injury or for other conditions. As such, the
ALJ finds that Claimant may select an authorized treating physician for
evaluation and treatment of his work-related shoulder injury.
Temporary Disability Benefits/Termination
P. To prove entitlement to temporary total disability (TTD), a claimant must prove
that the industrial injury caused a disability lasting more than three work shifts, he
left work because of the disability, and the disability resulted in an actual wage
loss. See §§ 8-42-103(1)(a) & (b) C.R.S.; Anderson v. Longmont Toyota, 102
P.3d 323 (Colo. 2004); City of Colorado Springs v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off.,
954 P.2d 637 (Colo. App. 1997). Section 8-42-103(1)(a) requires a claimant to
establish a causal connection between a work-related injury and a subsequent
wage loss to obtain temporary disability benefits. The term “disability” connotes
two elements: (1) medical incapacity evidenced by loss or restriction of bodily
function; and (2) impairment of wage-earning capacity as demonstrated by
claimant's inability to resume his or her prior work. Culver v. Ace Electric, 971
P.2d 641, 649 (Colo. 1999). The impairment of earning capacity element of
8

disability may be evidenced by a complete inability to work or by restrictions
which impair the claimant's ability effectively and properly to perform his or her
regular employment. Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy & Co., 964 P.2d 595, 597 (Colo.
App. 1998). Because there is no requirement that a claimant must produce
evidence of medical restrictions, a claimant’s testimony alone is sufficient to
demonstrate a disability. Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952 P.2d 831, 833 (Colo.
App. 1997).
Q. The Workers' Compensation Act prohibits a claimant from receiving temporary
disability benefits if the claimant is responsible for termination of the employment
relationship. Gilmore v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 187 P.3d 1129, (Colo. App.
2008); The termination statutes -- §§ 8-42-103(1)(g), 8-42-105(4)(a), C.R.S. --
provide: “In cases where it is determined that a temporarily disabled employee is
responsible for termination of employment, the resulting wage loss shall not be
attributable to the on-the-job injury.” See also In re of Davis, W.C. No. 4-631-681
(ICAO Apr. 24, 2006).
R. “Under the termination statutes, sections 8-42-103(1)(g) and 8-42-105(4), an
employer bears the burden of establishing by a preponderance of the evidence
that a claimant was terminated for cause or was responsible for the separation
from employment.” Gilmore, 187 P.3d at 1132. “Generally, the question of
whether the claimant acted volitionally, and therefore is ‘responsible’ for a
termination from employment, is a question of fact to be decided by the ALJ,
based on consideration of the totality of the circumstances.” Gonzales v. Indus.
Comm’n, 740 P.2d 999 (Colo. 1987); Windom v. Lawrence Constr. Co., W.C. No.
4-487-966 (ICAO Nov. 1, 2002). In re Olaes, WC. No. 4-782-977 (ICAO April 12,
2011). Implicit in the termination statutes is a requirement that Respondents
prove Claimant committed an “act” which formed the basis for her termination.
Ultimately, the question of whether the claimant was responsible for the
termination is one of fact for determination by the ALJ. Apex Trans., Inc. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Office, 321 P.3d 630, 632 (Colo. App. 2014).
S. Claimant has failed to establish an entitlement to temporary disability benefits,
and Employer has established that Claimant was responsible for his own
9

termination. After his initial evaluation at the UCHealth ER, Claimant was
released to return to work on April 15, 2025. Although Claimant was not subject
to work restrictions, Employer offered Claimant modified duty in writing, by asking
Claimant to come to the office to work on phone duty. Claimant elected not to
accept the modified employment and did not return to work for Employer
thereafter. Claimant then began new, full time employment with Valiant Products
Corporation on July 7, 2025. Claimant’s refusal to return to work for Employer
constitutes a voluntary resignation for which he was responsible. Claimant’s
wage loss is a result of his resignation, rather than his injury, and he is not
entitled to temporary disability benefits.
Penalties for Uninsured Employer
T. Section 8-43-408(1), C.R.S., provides that where an employer has not complied
with the Act’s insurance provisions, an injured worker may claim compensation
and benefits under the Act. Pursuant to section 8-43-408(2), C.R.S.: “In all cases
where compensation is awarded under the terms of this section, the director or
an administrative law judge of the division shall compute and require the
employer to pay to a trustee designated by the director or administrative law
judge an amount equal to the present value of all unpaid compensation or
benefits computed at the rate of four percent per annum; or, in lieu thereof, such
employer, within ten days after the date of such order, shall file a bond with the
director or administrative law judge signed by two or more responsible sureties to
be approved by the director or by some surety company authorized to do
business within the state of Colorado. The bond shall be in such form and
amount as prescribed and fixed by the director and shall guarantee the payment
of the compensation or benefits as awarded. The filing of any appeal, including a
petition for review, shall not relieve the employer of the obligation under this
subsection (2) to pay the designated sum to a trustee or to file a bond with the
director or administrative law judge.” The term “compensation” refers to disability
benefits. In Re of Shier, W.C. No. 4-573-910 (ICAO Dec. 15, 2005). Where an
employer is uninsured at the time of an injury; the provisions of section 8-43-
408(2) are mandatory.
10

U. Once a claimant establishes a compensable injury, the burden shifts to the
employer to establish a limitation of its liability by proof it had workers'
compensation insurance. McManus v. Oil Tools Limited, W.C. No. 4-481-926
(April 29, 2002). No credible evidence was admitted at hearing demonstrating
that Employer had in place workers’ compensation insurance at the time of
Claimant’s injury. Although Mr. Cheese’s statement and Mr. DeThomas’s text
messages imply that Employer was insured, Employer has not provided proof of
insurance and did not submit Claimant’s claim to an insurer. Section 8-43-103(1),
C.R.S., which requires employers to give notice to the Division and their
insurance carrier within ten days after an employee injury. Similarly, WCRP 5-
2(A), provides that an employer must report any work-related injury to the
employer’s insurer within ten days of notice or knowledge of the injury. The Rule
also provides that “An employer who does not provide the required notice may be
subject to penalties or other sanctions.”
V. Based on the evidence presented at hearing, the ALJ concludes that Employer
was uninsured at the time of Claimant’s injury and is obligated to either pay the
trustee or post a bond in the amount of the compensation and benefits to which
Claimant would be entitled.
W. Section 8-42-101 (3)(a)(I), C.R.S., provides that the fees charged by medical
providers for workers’ compensation injuries may not exceed those set forth in
the medical fee schedule adopted by the Director. No credible evidence was
admitted demonstrating that the fees charged by Claimant’s medical providers
comply with the fee schedule. Because the evidence was insufficient to
determine the amount of Claimant’s medical bills due under the Medical Fee
Schedule, the evidence is insufficient to determine the amount Employer is
required to pay to the trustee. This issue is reserved for future determination.
Additional Liability Under § 8-43-408(5), C.R.S.
A. Section 8-43-408(5), C.R.S., provides: In addition to any compensation paid or
ordered in accordance with this section or articles 40 to 47 of this title 8, an
employer who is not in compliance with the insurance provisions of those articles
at the time an employee suffers a compensable injury or occupational disease
11

shall pay an amount equal to twenty-five percent of the compensation or benefits
to which the employee is entitled to the Colorado uninsured employer fund
created in section 8-67-105.
B. Because the amount of compensation or benefits to which Claimant is entitled
cannot be determined based on the evidence presented, the ALJ cannot
determine Employer’s additional liability under § 8-43-408 (5), C.R.S. The issue
is reserved for future determination.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant sustained a compensable injury arising out of the course of his
employment with Employer on April 11, 2025.
2. Claimant is entitled to reasonable and necessary medical benefits to cure or
relieve the effects of his April 11, 2025 workplace injury. The treatment Claimant
received at UCHealth on April 11, 2025 was reasonable and necessary. Claimant
has failed to establish that the treatment he received from County Line
Chiropractic was reasonable, necessary, or related to his workplace injury.
3. Claimant is entitled to select his authorized treating physician for his workplace
injury.
4. Claimant’s request for temporary disability benefits is denied. Determination of
Claimant’s average weekly wage is moot.
5. Employer is liable for payment of Claimant’s medical expenses pursuant
to the Division of Workers’ Compensation Medical Fee Schedule. The
monetary amount of medical benefits is reserved for future determination,
and no payment is due until the benefits to which Claimant is entitled is
established. Because Employer is liable for payment of Claimant’s medical
costs associated with his work injury, no medical provider shall seek to
recover such costs from Claimant, pursuant to § 8-42-101(4), C.R.S.
a. In lieu of payment of the above compensation and benefits to the
Claimant, Employer shall:
12

b. Upon determination of the appropriate sum, deposit said sum with
the Division of Workers’ Compensation as trustee, to secure the
payment of all unpaid TTD benefits awarded. The check shall be
payable to and sent to the Division of Workers; Compensation
Division Trustee, c/o Mariya Cassin, 633 17th Street, Suite 400,
Denver, CO 80202; or
c. File a bond the Division of Workers’ Compensation within ten (10)
days of the date of any order determining amount of the
compensation and benefits to which Claimant is entitled:
i. Signed by two or more responsible sureties who have
received prior approval of the Division of Workers’
Compensation; or
ii. Issued by a surety company authorized to do business in
Colorado.
d. The bond shall guarantee payment of the compensation and benefit
awarded.
6. Employer is responsible for additional liability under § 8-43-408(5), C.R.S.,
for failure to maintain workers’ compensation insurance. Employer shall
pay the Colorado uninsured employer fund an amount equal to 25% of
compensation and benefits to which Claimant is entitled. The amount of
such additional liability is reserved for future determination, and no such
payment is due until the amount of additional liability has been
established.
7. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
NOTE: If you are dissatisfied with the ALJ's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,

13

mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. You may
